[11] It is my hope that this report can inspire a new way of thinking and formulating Danish foreign policy

[12] On September 15, 2015, I was asked to lead a study on Denmark's international engagement

[13] I have chosen to interpret the fact that the government has chosen to ask one person to lead the investigation – and not a committee of experts or civil servants – as meaning that the government wanted an investigation with an edge that opens up a political and popular debate

[14] This report is written in a time of turmoil in more than one sense

[15] The times are characterized by global power dispersion, demographic challenges and rapid technological development

[16] The European security order is challenged

[17] Europe's immediate region is characterized by recurring crises, while the EU's cohesion and ability to offer collective solutions are being tested

[18] Finally, the melting of the ice opens up the Arctic

[19] Incomparably, Danish diplomacy and defense – the primary foreign policy institutions in Denmark – are also in a time of struggle

[20] Both the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs have had decreasing appropriations under changing governments

[21] In a changing world, this requires prioritization, focus and effective representation of interests

[22] The government has asked for a proposal on Denmark's strategic interests, stronger integrated thinking and coordination of external policy areas, and Denmark's core tasks towards

[23] The report offers its opinion on these three things, but it is hoped that the report will serve as a starting point for a broad societal debate

[24] In a way, it has already succeeded

[25] During the investigative work, there has been a lively debate in the newspapers, on social media, on TV and during events at think tanks and interest groups around the country

Background analyses and data basis in a separate appendix volume of the foreign policy investigation Summary “Time of upheaval: … time of unrest and upheaval” Global spread of power, new threats and rapid technological development… In the coming years, Danish diplomacy and defense must operate in a world that is in many ways in a time of upheaval

[124] The economic center of gravity is shifting towards Asia, technological developments are changing the conditions for people, companies and authorities

[125] Europe's security and values ​​are being challenged, and the immediate area is characterized by crises and collapses, which are of great importance to Denmark

[126] The opportunities and challenges are many and varied, and the resources are limited at a time when Danish diplomacy and defense under changing governments have had decreasing funding

[127] In a changing world, this requires prioritization and effective representation of interests

[128] This calls for increased focus and integrated thinking of Denmark's efforts and reflection on which goals and tasks must be carried out first and foremost

[129] This report presents the results of the foreign and security policy review launched by the Government in September

[130] …creates a need for a fresh look at foreign policy priorities… According to the Terms of Reference, it should lead to three things

[131] An overview of Denmark's strategic interests in relation to a number of key development trends, challenges and opportunities in the coming 10-15 years

[132] A comprehensive proposal for stronger coordination and integrated thinking of Denmark's foreign and security policy, defense policy, trade policy and export promotion, and development policy

[133] A comprehensive strategic proposal for core tasks and priorities to promote Denmark's interests in the coming years. …and public debate on Denmark's role in the world

[134] According to the terms of reference, the purpose is to create the basis for increased focus and prioritization of Denmark's international engagement and the safeguarding of the Kingdom of Denmark's interests, including commercial ones

[135] How do we best position Denmark on the international stage in a time with limited resources for diplomacy and defense

[136] Cut to the bone, that is the question this study attempts to answer

[137] The report is a presentation for the political debate on future foreign and security policy and will, among other things, form the basis for the upcoming negotiations on a new defense agreement after 2017 and a new development policy strategy in 2016. Interest-based foreign policy The purpose of foreign policy is to contribute to understanding, influencing and relating to international developments with the main objective of preserving and further developing a safe, free and prosperous Denmark with a Danish value base for the benefit of the population

[138] Defense, security, development and trade policy are integrated parts of Denmark's foreign policy, which must fulfill this vision

[139] Foreign policy must safeguard Denmark's national interests and values. Based on the Kingdom of Denmark's distinctive features and position in the world

[140] This is best done by pursuing an interest-based, coordinated and focused foreign policy that has the security, prosperity and fundamental values 'of Denmark, the other parts of the kingdom and the population as its central guiding principles

[141] The starting point is the lasting relationships that are linked to Denmark's position in the world and role as an international player, the reality that surrounds us, and the values ​​on which Danish society is built

[142] The Kingdom of Denmark is an Arctic power and a smaller European country located between the regional powers and part of a Nordic and Northern European cultural circle

[143] Denmark is also a trading nation with a small open economy that thrives best in a stable and regular international order

[144] Denmark's membership of the EU, NATO and the UN is the fundamental foundation for safeguarding Denmark's interests internationally

[145] the foreign policy report... establishes a prioritization tool for effective protection of interests. However, national interests cannot stand alone

[146] A focused foreign policy must also take into account how Denmark can ensure the greatest possible impact

[147] Strategic choices should therefore be based on a balance of three considerations in particular: ▪▪

[148] Interests: What is at stake for Denmark

[149] Is this a vital, very important or less important national interest

[150] Is a Danish interest threatened by the development

[151] Partnerships: Is this a uniquely Danish or a broadly shared interest

[152] Can we do it alone or in partnerships with others

[153] Should Denmark take the lead

[154] Or can we leave the task to our partners

[155] Can we make a difference

[156] Are there particular Danish strengths, expertise or experiences in demand

[157] These three considerations can form the core of a prioritization tool for a more strategic utilization of Danish foreign policy resources, focusing efforts on the areas where we have the most at stake and can make the biggest difference – either alone or in partnerships

[158] Some interests Denmark will have to pursue alone, others are shared by many and are best pursued together

[159] The specific assessment must be based on an analysis of the challenges and opportunities that Denmark and other countries face

[160] Over the next 10-15 years, Denmark will have to navigate a world that will differ significantly in several areas from the past 25 years after the Cold War

[161] In parallel with globalization and the spread of cross-border networks, traditional geopolitics and thus geographical location will once again become more important

[162] Greater unpredictability becomes a pervasive condition in a more connected world, where power is spread across multiple hands, and technological quantum leaps lead to both new opportunities and risks

[163] The world is becoming more unpredictable. In many places things are going historically well…

[164] Overall, the world is moving in a more peaceful and prosperous direction

[165] Since 1990, the number of extremely poor people has more than halved, and the global middle class has tripled

[166] More countries are integrating into the world economy, and significant progress is being made in, among other things, access to health and education. … but Europe is challenged on several fronts and risks closing in on itself even more. However, Europe's neighboring areas with Russia to the east and the Middle East to the south pose increasing challenges

[167] The European security order is under pressure from Russia, and the Middle East and North Africa will continue to be a significant source of instability with direct effects for Europe and Denmark

[168] This is due to conflicts, militant extremism, poor governance and refugee flows

[169] Afghanistan and parts of Africa could also be sources of continued instability

[170] Despite a generally more stable world, Europe's neighboring regions face serious challenges in the coming years

[171] At the same time, Europe is experiencing increasing nationalism and Euroscepticism, which will contribute to a more inward-looking EU in the coming years

[172] And the EU will probably continue to have difficulty translating its global economic weight into corresponding foreign policy impact

[173] In the Arctic, the melting of the ice opens up prospects for increased economic activity and development, but also increases the need for government tasks such as sea rescue and environmental protection

[174] the foreign policy report Economic growth in Asia is gradually shifting the global political and economic center of gravity from west to east

[175] This will also make the rest of the world more dependent on continued economic growth and stability in the region, especially in China

[176] Global trade towards 2030 will be characterized by a number of trends that will have great significance for Denmark

[177] This includes increased trade with and in Asia, integration of developing countries into the global economy, growth in trade in services, and deeper globalization, where complex trade flows in so-called value chains increase the need for global cooperation and trade policy rules

[178] The economic center of gravity is shifting towards Asia and more are integrating into the world economy

[179] There are more and more of us on the planet... The world's population will reach around 8.5 billion in 2030, and population growth will occur especially in large cities, which will become more important as global players

[180] Growth and job opportunities for millions of young people will be crucial for social stability, mobility and migration in areas of population growth

[181] At the same time, Europe will experience increasing labor shortages

[182] Climate change will be a threat multiplier that will contribute to instability and migration

[183] At the same time, the new climate agreement obliges all countries to intensify the fight against climate change and creates great opportunities for Danish exports

[184] Innovation and the spread of new technologies are occurring at an increasing rate and are fundamentally changing markets, forms of communication and workflows

[185] The Internet will make the world even more interconnected and provide new economic opportunities, while cyber threats will pose a growing security policy challenge. …and technology binds us closer together and changes our everyday lives. International stability will increasingly depend on the relationship between the US and China, while the EU and strong states such as India and Brazil can also play a greater role on the international stage

[186] The combined economic, military, political and cultural strength of the United States and Europe will continue to have a stabilizing global influence until

[187] But the new, strong states want greater influence on international political and economic decisions

[188] It is therefore crucial that a rules-based international order continues to be maintained, which both the states that are moving up the international hierarchy accept and act in, and which other countries can also see themselves in

[189] Overall, the development will shift the global balance of power… …and non-state actors will gain greater importance

[190] At the same time, an increasing number of challenges will exceed the capabilities of states and require new and broader societal alliances

[191] Non-state actors such as cities, provinces, multinational corporations, foundations, informal groups and powerful individuals will gain increased global influence

[192] A wider range of actors will therefore want a seat at the table when international decisions are made

[193] Globalization is accelerating a diffusion of power, where states no longer have a monopoly on foreign and security policy

[194] National governments and international institutions will increasingly find that there will be developments that they cannot predict and have no control over

[195] In that situation, effective international responses will depend on the strength and breadth of international and societal partnerships

[196] Denmark's future foreign and security policy

[197] The changed global context creates both challenges and opportunities for Denmark

[198] Foreign policy efforts must be prioritized strictly according to interests, positions of strength and opportunities for partnerships

[199] This applies to both multilateral and bilateral efforts and the individual policy areas and instruments in foreign, security, development, trade and defense policy

[200] The fundamental purposes of diplomacy will remain unchanged

[201] But the instruments must be adapted as the topics become more diverse, interconnected, and new actors enter the scene

[202] At the same time, the resource framework is being narrowed, also in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs

[203] From 2000 to 2019, the foreign service will be cut by a third or approximately DKK 800 million. International developments combined with a general decrease in funding require increased prioritization and reinforce the need for the involvement of other actors in foreign policy

[204] The tasks must be carried out with a smaller foreign service......that is at the forefront of developments. The increased unpredictability also requires an adaptable and open foreign service that is able to analyze and be at the forefront of developments and create added value for the entire spectrum of Danish interest representation

[205] The ability to combine traditional diplomatic channels with formal and informal networks becomes a pivotal point

[206] It is a strength here that the overall responsibility for foreign policy analysis for diplomacy, development assistance, export promotion and trade policy is concentrated in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which also handles the increased tasks of citizen services and emergency preparedness as well as public diplomacy and communication in relations with foreign countries

[207] by virtue of its employees and local presence… As the coordinating authority in the foreign affairs area, it is important that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs can recruit and retain employees with international experience and expertise while maintaining the necessary mobility in the service

[208] Through the representations, Denmark must have a sufficiently strong presence in the policy-making capitals with the greatest importance for Danish interests

[209] and in close cooperation with the EU's Common Foreign and Security Service. Conversely, in countries where we are not present ourselves, Denmark must take the consequences and entrust tasks that do not have a particularly Danish character to the EU's Common Foreign and Security Service or other partners

[210] An analysis of Denmark's future foreign service should be prepared that addresses these issues

[211] The Ministry of Foreign Affairs must be the international liaison for the entire society

[212] Strategic focus should be ensured so that efforts and resources are used where Denmark has the most at stake

[213] This will create the best conditions for making a difference, alone or with others

[214] This allows us to influence the world in the direction that best aligns with Danish interests and values. Multilateral efforts Denmark has great advantages in binding international cooperation and rules that ensure influence for smaller countries and common rules of the game

[271] Development policy, stabilization and economic diplomacy With the new global goals and the Paris climate agreement, the stage has been set for an unprecedented close race between public and private actors to mobilize resources for selected focus areas

[272] This means, for example, that green transition and sustainable urbanization will become both development goals and growth sectors for business

A stronger link between development cooperation and Danish interests can be achieved by focusing efforts within three areas of focus

[281] Promoting sustainable growth and development

[282] Strengthen efforts in countries in fragile situations

[283] Prevent refugee and migration flows Sustainable growth must be promoted through partnerships with developing and emerging countries, business and private investors, so that development assistance is used to a greater extent as risk capital and leverage for private investments and sharing of Danish experiences and solutions

[284] Traditional country programs should gradually be transformed into more flexible partnerships, where assistance serves as a catalyst for other sources of funding and supports Danish commercial interests

[285] Aid must be a lever for sustainable growth and development. In relation to fragile states and migration, closer coordination of humanitarian aid, development cooperation, stabilization efforts and Danish positions of strength must contribute to addressing the problems closer to their origin

[312] The future orientation of the Danish Armed Forces The tasks of the Danish Armed Forces are laid down in the Defence Act, while the framework of defence policy is regulated via a five-year agreement

[313] The report will form the basis for negotiations on the next defense agreement

[314] Denmark's surrounding areas have become less safe, and threats have moved closer

[315] an increased conventional military threat to Danish territory remains unlikely, but the surrounding areas of Denmark and Europe have become less secure

[316] Geographically, the threats from terrorism and fragile states have moved closer, and Russia's actions are undermining the European security order and adding a threat dimension that was not foreseen a few years ago

[317] In addition, there is the increased cyber threat, and the melting of the ice in the Arctic means that the defense needs increased authority tasks....and the need for the defense's contribution to both international and national tasks is increasing. Considerations about the future development of the defense must therefore take into account the tightened security policy conditions

[318] There is both an increased need for international military contributions, including to NATO's credible deterrence capability, and increased national tasks, including civil and military exercise of authority, as well as increased authority tasks in the Arctic

[319] There is a need to continue to develop a set of robust military capabilities that are flexible and that, together with our allies, can be used across the full spectrum of missions, including for real deterrence and very high-intensity activities against a capable adversary

[320] The defense must be able to operate effectively with Denmark's closest allies

[321] It is crucial that Danish military forces are able to operate effectively with core allies

[322] Denmark cannot and should not operate alone in international operations, and there should be a forward-looking focus on cooperation, also within the Nordic framework and with countries around the Baltic Sea

[323] Denmark has a long tradition of pursuing an activist security policy with significant contributions to international military operations

[324] This has made Denmark a recognized partner and ally and given it influence in the UN, the EU and especially NATO, although Denmark's influence is weakened by the defense reservation

[325] NATO is the cornerstone of Denmark's security policy and ultimately Denmark's security guarantee

[326] NATO must continuously find a balance between its three core tasks - collective defense, crisis management through international operations, and partnerships

[327] Denmark must contribute to ensuring that there is sufficient focus on all these tasks and that the alliance is able to ensure sufficient military deterrence without losing focus on the other tasks

[328] NATO's strength and impact depend on the political will and the resources that individual countries allocate to defense

[329] In Wales, NATO countries took stock of the heightened threat picture and began an adaptation of the alliance, including increased focus on reassurance of the eastern allies

[330] The NATO countries, like Denmark, which are below NATO's 2% target for defense spending as a share of GDP, have committed to stopping the decline in spending, striving for real growth and, in the long term, striving to spend 2% of GDP on defense....and Denmark must remain a core ally in NATO and continue to contribute actively. Denmark's defense spending has fallen since the Cold War because the favorable security policy situation made it possible to use the funds in areas other than defense

[331] We are now in a new situation with significant changes in Denmark's and Europe's security policy conditions

[332] Denmark is the only country in the Baltic Sea region that has not responded to the new situation with plans for increased defense spending, and with a continued decline, it will hardly be possible in the long-term to maintain Denmark's current position among the top in the alliance in terms of being able to deliver contributions to NATO's core tasks

[333] After a number of favorable years where savings could be made, we are now in a new situation. There is a need to break the curve and add more resources to the defense. The price of Denmark's insurance policy has increased, and there is a need to add more resources to the defense so that Denmark can continue to contribute in solidarity and credibly to the security of Europe and thus Denmark

[334] Denmark should therefore break the curve and stop the downward trend in defense spending and - during the next defense settlement period - increase the defense budget as a share of GDP in accordance with Denmark's NATO commitments

The way forward for Denmark's interests and values should be an interest-based foreign policy that - based on Denmark's strategic orientation - focuses and gathers forces where the stakes are highest and where Denmark can make a real difference

[356] Core tasks and priorities International developments combined with the implementation of significant savings in the foreign and security policy area create a need to prioritize and focus efforts to ensure optimal protection of Denmark's interests

[357] On this basis, five benchmarks can be identified for Denmark's external policy areas: …and focus on the most important tasks for Denmark ▪

[358] The immediate area: Actively promote sustainable and peaceful development in the Kingdom's immediate areas in the Arctic and Baltic Sea region by prioritizing efforts and strengthening and developing cooperation structures as well as the capacity to be at the forefront of opportunities and threats

[359] Europe: Take responsibility for peace, stability and prosperity in Europe and Europe's surrounding areas by, in particular, actively contributing to an EU that is able to collectively handle crises and exercise global influence, contribute to the fight against terrorism and secure Denmark's position as a core member of credible NATO cooperation and as a transatlantic bridge builder

[360] Refugees and migration

[361] Prevent uncontrolled flows by strengthening the integration of foreign policy, regional interventions, stabilization efforts, humanitarian assistance and long-term development cooperation to promote security, economic development and good governance, especially in fragile states in the Middle East, North Africa and Afghanistan

[362] ▪ Economic diplomacy: Contribute to Danish growth, prosperity and innovation by conducting active economic diplomacy that positions Denmark strongly in the rapid business development, supports the internationalization, competitiveness and exports of the business community and society's ability to attract investments, knowledge and talents from all over the world

[363] ▪ Global goods: Promote global solutions and handling of future climate challenges by, based on Danish positions of strength, values and interests, taking the lead in implementing the UN 2030 Agenda and the Paris Climate Agreement and supporting rules-based international cooperation, where both old and new powers will continue to see the UN as the primary global framework for balancing interests

[364] These five guiding principles constitute a comprehensive strategic proposal for core tasks and priorities to promote Denmark's interests

[365] Within these areas, initiatives should be prioritized based on criteria of where there is something at stake for Denmark, whether we can make a difference, and whether it is a narrow or broad interest. Integrated thinking and coordination of Denmark's foreign policy The five guiding principles largely cross traditional distinctions between foreign, security, defense, trade, and development policy

[396] Introduction Danish diplomacy and defense in a time of struggle Danish diplomacy and defense must operate in the coming years in a world that is in many ways in a time of struggle

[397] The economic center of gravity is shifting towards Asia, technological development is changing the conditions for people, companies and authorities, Europe's security and values ​​are being challenged, and the immediate area is characterized by crises and collapses, which are of great importance to Denmark

[398] The opportunities and challenges are many and varied, and resources are limited

[399] This calls for increased focus and integrated thinking in Denmark's efforts and, not least, reflection on which goals and tasks must be carried out first and foremost

[400] This report constitutes the result of the foreign policy investigation launched by the government on 15 September

[401] The investigation was conducted under the leadership of Ambassador Peter Taksøe-Jensen with secretarial assistance from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of Defense

[402] According to the Terms of Reference for the investigation, the investigation work must lead to three things: How was the investigation carried out

[403] The report is based on extensive analysis and data collected over the past six months

[404] These include existing reports and analyses from Danish and foreign sources, as well as a number of analyses that have been prepared specifically to support the investigation work

[405] In addition, a number of previous Danish foreign policy studies, reports and strategies have been revisited

[406] They span several decades and thus different foreign and security policy eras

[407] This has made it possible to draw common threads in Danish foreign policy

[408] As part of the work, a follow-up group has been established with 20 members from the research community and organizations with special insight into the area

[409] The follow-up group has held a total of four meetings focusing on various foreign and security policy themes and development trends

[410] The follow-up group's discussions have served as significant input to the investigation, but the report's conclusions and recommendations are the sole responsibility of the investigator

[411] Furthermore, a large number of meetings and debate events have been held with experts and stakeholders in the foreign and security policy area, including politicians, industry organizations, researchers, civil society organizations, etc

[412] In accordance with the terms of reference, the investigator has held meetings with the rapporteurs of the political parties and with the established foreign policy forums

[413] With a view to ensuring the involvement of Greenland and the Faroe Islands, meetings have been held in Nuuk and Copenhagen with a focus on developments in the Arctic

[414] The discussions form part of the basis for the study's analysis of the Arctic

[415] As part of the information gathering, the investigator has visited The Hague, London, Brussels, Washington, New York, Geneva, Berlin and Beijing in chronological order

[416] The purpose has been to gather inspiration from similar studies, discuss international developments in both a bilateral and multilateral context, and discuss cooperation with some of Denmark's most important partners

[417] An identification of Denmark's strategic interests in light of a number of key development trends, challenges and opportunities in the coming 10-15 years, A comprehensive proposal for stronger coordination and integrated thinking of Denmark's foreign and security policy, defense policy, trade policy and export promotion, and development policy

[418] A comprehensive strategic proposal for core tasks and priorities to promote Denmark's interests in the coming years

[419] According to the terms of reference, the purpose is to create the basis for increased focus and prioritization of the Kingdom of Denmark's international engagement and the safeguarding of the Kingdom's interests, including commercial ones

[420] The study constitutes a basis for the political debate on future foreign and security policy and will, among other things, form the basis for the upcoming negotiations on a new defense agreement after 2017 and a new development policy strategy in

[421] Denmark conducts foreign and security policy on behalf of the entire Kingdom, that is, on behalf of Denmark, the Faroe Islands and Greenland

[422] Therefore, reference is made to the Kingdom, the Kingdom and the Commonwealth where relevant in this context

[423] The report will present a comprehensive, strategic proposal for strengthened prioritization, focus, and integrated thinking of Denmark's broad foreign and security policy commitment over seven chapters

[424] Chapter 1 presents a model for a more interest-based foreign policy and a prioritization tool for foreign policy efforts

[425] The chapter also provides a suggestion for the fixed conditions that characterize Denmark as a foreign policy actor, and which are the starting point for determining Denmark's vital and very important national interests, which foreign policy must primarily foster

[426] Chapter 2 uncovers the key global and regional development trends, challenges and opportunities that will shape the international reality that Denmark must navigate towards

[427] Chapters 1 and 2 together form the basis for the subsequent chapters on the planning of Denmark's future foreign and security policy: Chapter 3 focuses on the Ministry of Foreign Affairs' instruments, frameworks and efforts in a more interconnected and unpredictable world

[428] As a coordinating authority, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs must function as the international link for the entire society and be able to bring added value to the entire spectrum of Danish interest representation abroad

[429] Chapter 4 uncovers

[430] Denmark's strategic interests and efforts in a multilateral, bilateral and cross-border perspective

[431] The chapter suggests where Denmark in particular has interests at stake and should therefore focus on multilateral and bilateral engagement

[432] Chapter 5 offers a proposal for innovative thinking and strengthened coordination of Denmark's global engagement in the form of development policy, stabilization efforts and economic diplomacy

[433] The SDGs are presented as a common benchmark for future efforts, and a proposal for ten guidelines for a new development policy strategy is given

[434] Chapter 6 provides a proposal for the future tasks and organization of the Danish Armed Forces based on a security and defense policy analysis and a description of the framework for task performance

[435] The chapter has been prepared with a view to forming part of the basis for the upcoming defence settlement negotiations

[436] Chapter 7 brings together the threads from the previous chapters into five future core tasks and their realization through increased integration of foreign policy instruments

[437] The chapter presents a proposal for mechanisms that can ensure strategic coordination across authorities and policy areas and a political and popular anchoring that can strengthen continuity in foreign policy

An interest-based, integrated and focused foreign policy 1.1 Denmark's position in the world Chapter 1 sets out an interest-based model for foreign policy that can serve as a guideline for strategic choices and priorities in the coming years

[445] Together with the global development trends outlined in Chapter 2, the interest-based model will form the basis for the identification of Denmark's strategic interests and efforts in the following chapters

[446] The Kingdom of Denmark is at the same time a smaller European country and, by virtue of the Commonwealth with the Faroe Islands and Greenland, an Arctic power and the world's 12th largest territory, which has special interests and obligations in the North Atlantic and the Arctic

[447] Denmark's relations with the outside world have historically been conditioned by our geographical location between regional powers such as Great Britain, Germany and Russia and by our control over the straits that provide access to and from the Baltic Sea

[448] Denmark is also part of a Nordic and Northern European cultural community, which is reflected in the values on which our society is built: Denmark is a free, open and democratic society governed by the rule of law

[449] Denmark is a trading and maritime nation with a small, open economy that is highly specialized and deeply integrated into a worldwide network of economic relations

[450] In addition, Denmark is an innovative knowledge society, leading in a number of areas where the world is increasingly demanding solutions

[451] Exports account for over half of Denmark's GDP, but Denmark's economy accounts for less than half a percent of the world economy

[452] Our prosperity depends on our access to trade and investment across borders

[453] We must therefore organize ourselves and our foreign policy in a way that best utilizes the opportunities that internationalization offers – both by influencing abroad and by understanding and adapting to changes in the world

[454] Due to the Kingdom's size, location and open economy, Denmark is a country that thrives best in a regular and predictable international order

[455] This order is not a given, but a result of the fact that, after two devastating world wars, the United States and European countries in particular have established and joined binding communities that have a stabilizing effect politically, in terms of security and economically

[456] Denmark's membership of the EU, NATO and the UN is the fundamental foundation for safeguarding Denmark's interests internationally

[457] The EU and NATO are the central forums for safeguarding Denmark's interests and security

[458] Supranational cooperation in the EU ensures stable relations between European countries and at the same time contributes to safeguarding Denmark's political and economic interests in Europe and the world

[459] NATO and the transatlantic cooperation with the United States are ultimately Denmark's security guarantee

[460] Globalization presents Denmark and Europe with significant challenges that individual countries cannot solve individually

[461] The binding European cooperation in the EU is therefore, together with NATO, a fundamental framework condition for promoting Denmark's national interests and for Denmark's prosperity, freedom and security

[462] These relatively constant and specific characteristics of Denmark help shape the basic conditions on the basis of which Denmark must conduct its foreign policy

[463] Together, they constitute a natural starting point for identifying the Danish national interests that foreign policy must uphold

[464] The purpose and method of foreign policy to contribute to international development that both ensures Denmark a strong economic base and contributes to positive, responsible and balanced development in our world

[465] If goals and efforts are coordinated and implemented across authorities and across society as a whole, they will have a much greater effect than individual, uncoordinated initiatives

[466] Stronger integrated thinking across authorities and society as a whole requires clear guidelines

[467] An identification of Danish national interests is a way of clarifying the goals that foreign policy efforts should pursue

[468] It can and should be a central part of a continuous steering instrument in foreign policy

[469] This requires that the determination of interests is based on the more or less fixed framework conditions and values that apply to Denmark

[470] The purpose of the Kingdom of Denmark's foreign policy is to understand, influence and respond to international developments with a view to preserving and further developing a secure, free and prosperous Denmark and the Danish values ​​for the benefit of the population

[471] Defense, security, development and trade policy are integrated parts of Denmark's foreign policy, which must fulfill this vision

[472] Denmark must exercise its influence where international developments challenge the realization of these goals

[473] And where the influence is most effective, because it can make a difference. The foreign policy method that should support the purpose is an interest-based, coherent and focused foreign policy that ensures Denmark's greatest possible impact in the areas where the most is at stake for Denmark and the population. The starting point for Denmark's foreign policy should therefore be a determination of Denmark's fundamental foreign and security policy interests

[474] In continuation of this, there must be prioritization and delimitation, so that we focus our efforts where the most is at stake and where it makes the biggest difference

[475] Over time, Denmark has built a free, secure and prosperous society

[476] We have done this on the basis of societal values and principles of cooperation, social dialogue, equality, openness and trust

[477] And we have been able to do so because Denmark has been privileged to be part of and actively contribute to a Europe and a world that, since the Second World War and until recently, has formed an increasingly secure framework for peace and prosperity

[478] Denmark thrives best in a stable, liberal and regular world order and best defends Danish interests and values ​​by contributing to a rules-based international system

[479] By virtue of the Commonwealth with the Faroe Islands and Greenland, the Kingdom has special opportunities and responsibilities in the Arctic

[480] Denmark, the Faroe Islands and Greenland stand in the Commonwealth far stronger than the sum of the influence of each part of the kingdom

[481] This means that cohesion and common goals in the region are the best starting point for influencing the development that is underway in the Arctic for the benefit of the Kingdom, the region and the people of Greenland and the Faroe Islands

[482] For many years, Denmark has contributed and must continue to contribute to pulling the world in a direction that benefits the population and what Denmark stands for

[483] But the outside world has also given Denmark ideas, opportunities and knowledge that we make use of and which have made us strong

[484] Denmark has thus been largely shaped – and has benefited – from the outside world, and we must continue to understand developments in the world around us

[485] This is the prerequisite for us to be able to influence and adapt to the reality around us

[486] At the same time, Denmark's foreign and security policy does not only encompass the Kingdom's military and diplomatic capacity

[487] in the areas we choose to prioritize

[488] also depends on our ability to draw on the strength of the entire society. 1.3 Denmark's national interests and values ​​Denmark's foreign policy must safeguard the national interests of the Kingdom

[489] This is done most effectively by pursuing an interest-based foreign policy that has the security, prosperity and fundamental values ​​of Denmark, the other parts of the kingdom and the population as its central guiding principles

[490] The Danish values ​​are therefore also to be considered part of the Kingdom's interests

[491] An interest-based approach does not rest on a contradiction between values ​​and interests

[492] On the contrary, Denmark's national interests largely stem from the values ​​and principles on which Danish society is built and which we wish to preserve and defend

[493] Denmark must therefore continue to base its foreign policy and cooperation with partners, both within and outside the EU, on the values ​​and principles that are central to the Danish social model

[494] Maintaining a rules-based international order that provides clarity about the common rules of the game and protects fundamental human rights is in Denmark's interest

[495] Respect for the rule of law and good governance in the countries with which Denmark and Danish companies cooperate is in Denmark's interest, and also contributes to protecting Danish citizens when they travel abroad

[496] Maintaining democracy and cooperation within the EU is also in Denmark's interest

[497] Regardless of how Denmark's foreign policy is organized, and regardless of the relationship between interests and values, Denmark will continue to find itself in situations of conflict between different interests, values and principles

[498] In these cases, it will continue to be a political consideration as to how the various considerations should be balanced

[499] As argued in section 4.1.4, a clearly defined and communicated value policy profile can serve as a guideline for weighing up different considerations and create predictability about Denmark's positions and key issues

[500] Determining the overall vision and priorities for foreign policy is fundamentally a political issue

[501] An interest-based foreign policy should not be seen as an expression of a specific political or ideological direction

[502] On the contrary, it is a model for a more systematic and reasoned approach in a changing world where the need to concentrate Denmark's resources is increasing

[503] This can create greater foreign policy continuity and impact

[504] When foreign policy cannot safeguard all Danish interests, it is relevant to ask: Which interests and values ​​are the most important for Denmark to protect and further develop

[505] And where and how can it be done with the greatest effect

[506] by an interest-based foreign policy Why should Denmark pursue an interest-based foreign policy

[507] First, we must make the most of the resources available to conduct foreign policy – ​​regardless of whether the budgets are large or small

[508] This calls for prioritizing Denmark's efforts internationally, and prioritization calls for clear direction: a set of well-considered and lasting national interests

[509] Without a set of clear, prioritized and lasting goals, the foreign policy course risks becoming unfocused and ad hoc

[510] Secondly, an interest-based foreign policy could function as a common frame of reference for politicians and the population when decisions have to be made

[511] A foreign policy approach based on a shared understanding of the Kingdom's national interests could help focus the debate and justify why Denmark should prioritize a given effort over others

[512] This will thus contribute to ensuring broad political and popular support for foreign policy decisions

[513] Thirdly, an interest-based foreign policy will more clearly reflect the connection between foreign policy and domestic policy and the fact that developments outside Denmark's borders and Denmark's handling of or adaptation to them have a large impact on conditions within Denmark

[514] It will also highlight the places where it will have a greater effect to use foreign policy resources than domestic policy ones

[515] Finally, an interest-based approach is a good starting point for a more integrated foreign policy, because the defined interests function as common directional arrows for all efforts across the various external policy areas

[516] But national interests can only serve as a guide for the foreign policy course if Denmark is aware of its national interests and has the courage to identify what is in the interest of the Kingdom and the population, and what is not

[517] It requires opt-ins as well as opt-outs

[518] And it requires a recognition that something is more important than something else, and that some efforts must therefore take precedence over others

[519] How are Denmark's interests determined

[520] At the most basic level, in order to be considered a Danish interest, an issue must have a clear relationship to the Kingdom of Denmark

[521] In other words, Denmark must have something at stake in the issue in question in the sense that the matter has the potential to influence the Kingdom, its citizens, companies, organizations, allies or the like, positively or negatively

[522] This does not mean that Denmark cannot have a position on or a policy to influence issues that fall outside this definition

[523] It will not be possible to avoid it at all

[524] But greater Danish efforts on matters in which Denmark has no particular stake will not be an expression of a strong connection between Denmark's efforts and Denmark's national interests

[525] Such prioritization will therefore not be an expression of effective representation of Danish interests

[526] Determining what is in Denmark's interest, what is not, and what weighs more heavily than anything else is a difficult exercise

[527] For how can one weigh a peace plan for the Middle East against development in Africa, export promotion in China, combating cross-border terrorism, cybercrime or global warming

[528] With the following method, Denmark's interests can be determined on a sober basis with three elements

[529] First, the fundamental interest in Denmark must be defined

[530] It is ultimately a political choice to make this definition

[531] However, this report is based on the following definition: "Denmark's fundamental interest is to preserve and further develop a secure, free and prosperous Denmark with a Danish foundation of values ​​for the benefit of the population

[532] Secondly, if one takes this fundamental interest and Denmark's position in the world as a starting point, a number of prioritized interests in foreign policy can be derived and established

[533] These priority interests are divided into categories, thirdly, according to their importance for the fulfilment of the defined fundamental interest

[534] This study is based on the following vital and very important interests, which have been attempted to be defined based on relatively lasting and broadly based characteristics of the Kingdom of Denmark, including the Danish social model and the Danish value sets

[535] Vital interests are defined as "conditions that are crucial for preserving and further developing a safe, free and prosperous Denmark with a Danish value base for the benefit of the population

[536] “Very important interests are defined as “matters that are of great importance or can affect the possibility of maintaining and further developing a safe, free and prosperous Denmark with a Danish value base for the benefit of the population”

[537] When security policy interests weigh particularly heavily in the group of vital interests, it does not mean that security policy efforts should take up the majority of Denmark's foreign policy resources

[538] On the contrary, it is an expression of the fact that certain fundamental and universal nation-state interests are the entire prerequisite for the maintenance of all other interests

[539] In practice, the Kingdom's security interests will be safeguarded directly through, among other things, NATO cooperation and more indirectly through the political and economic integration between countries and the global structures that maintain a stable world order and regulate coexistence between countries

[540] Precisely for this reason, there will be room and resources to nurture other, less existential interests in the daily prioritization of Denmark's foreign policy efforts

[541] At the same time, there is also the synergy between the interests that important interests in trade and exports, sustainable economic development and efforts to develop and stabilize abroad are also a long-term prerequisite for being able to invest in and safeguard Denmark's security policy interests

[542] The goal must therefore be to organize the efforts in such a way that there is as little conflict as possible and as much synergy as possible between the different interests and efforts

[543] Here, integrated thinking across initiatives and policy areas plays a central role

[544] Denmark conducts foreign and security policy on behalf of the entire Realm, that is, on behalf of Denmark, the Faroe Islands and Greenland, and an attempt has been made in relevant passages to refer to the Realm and the Kingdom of Denmark

[545] Prioritization tool** Denmark's vital interests are ▪▪ to ensure

[546] The continued existence, integrity and security of the kingdom

[547] ▪▪ ensure continued peaceful coexistence between European powers through the EU and NATO

[548] counter attacks that threaten the maintenance of vital societal functions counteract development trends that could decisively undermine the Danish social model

[549] ▪▪ ensure the necessary conditions for a sustainable Danish economy that can maintain our independence and cohesion in the long term

[550] ▪▪ ensure well-functioning international structures that regulate the actions of states and establish a framework for global conflict management

[551] Denmark's very important interests are to promote stability and cooperation in the Kingdom of Denmark's immediate area through dialogue and well-functioning European and transatlantic cooperation and security structures

[552] ▪▪ protect Denmark, the population and our allies against serious terrorist attacks

[553] ▪▪ assist Danish citizens abroad in the event of crises and serious incidents

[554] ensure our access to global economic networks, including markets, investment opportunities, transportation routes, labor, and the ability to conduct financial transactions uphold and promote the rule of law, human rights, and the right of all countries to determine their own alliances and social structures

[555] ▪ contribute to global development, stability and sustainable growth to reduce poverty, conflicts, radicalization, migration and refugee flows ▪

[556] ▪ contribute to reducing climate change and mitigating its negative consequences

[557] ▪▪ ensure the reputation of the Kingdom of Denmark abroad, including that we are perceived by close allies as a trustworthy partner with the ability and willingness to defend our territory, integrity and vital interests

[558] Based on the determination of Denmark's national interests, it is possible to take a step further by establishing criteria for more strategic prioritization in foreign policy

[559] Strategic choices and priorities should be based on a balance of three considerations in particular

[560] Interests: What is at stake for Denmark

[561] Is this a vital, very important or less important national interest

[562] Is a Danish interest threatened by the development

[563] Partnerships: Is this a uniquely Danish or a broadly shared interest

[564] Can we do it alone or in partnerships with others

[565] Should Denmark take the lead

[566] Or can we leave it to others

[567] Can we make a difference

[568] Are there particular Danish strengths, expertise or experiences in demand

[569] These three considerations can form the core of a prioritization tool for a more strategic utilization of Danish foreign policy resources, focusing efforts on the areas where we have the most at stake and can make the biggest difference – either alone or in partnerships

[570] The Netherlands and Norway have worked with similar models to ensure strategic foreign policy priorities

[571] Step 1 serves for an initial rough sorting of the topics according to importance, i.e. the above model for determining Denmark's national interests

[572] Safeguarding the vital interests of the Kingdom will by definition be a "need to do" in foreign and security policy, just as very important interests are considered instrumental for safeguarding the vital ones

[573] But the further away you get from vital interests, the more there is a need to prioritize the topics (“important to do” or “nice to do”

[574] The next two steps – partnerships and influence – can therefore serve as additional, guiding criteria for strategic choices among foreign policy efforts

[575] The question of uniquely Danish versus broad, shared interests serves to determine whether there are opportunities for alliances and partnerships through which Denmark can achieve greater impact

[576] Or whether strategic division of labor can be sought between partners, whereby Denmark does not actively pursue a given topic, but leaves it to others

[577] An example of a unique Danish interest is the handling of the Kingdom's territorial claims to the seabed in the Polar Ocean, which are not handled by anyone other than Denmark

[578] Broadly shared interests are often linked to global public goods such as a stable climate, but can also be narrower, such as the common interest of European countries in the appropriate management of refugee and migration flows

[579] As a smaller country that is closely intertwined with and dependent on international economic and political systems, Denmark will often have a significant stake in the broadly shared interests

[580] But that does not mean that Denmark can or should always play an active role

[581] As a third step, it should be considered whether Denmark can actually exert influence in the area –

[582] either alone or with others

[583] Here it will be important to look at whether there are special openings that allow Denmark to move an issue forward or influence a balance in the right direction

[584] Whether Denmark has special conditions to play a constructive role, and whether there is a match with Danish positions of strength

[585] This prioritization tool can serve as a useful guide for strategic choices and opt-outs in foreign policy

[586] Both for the overall organization of Denmark's foreign and security policy priorities

[587] But also ongoing concrete weighing of efforts and priorities within individual areas of concern

[588] Coordinated efforts towards common goals** The traditionally broad political support for the foreign policy pursued and efficient decision-making processes mean that Denmark can often act quickly and effectively

[589] This gives us a comparative advantage in a time of complex challenges

[590] But it can get even better

[591] The possibility of strategic thinking is often challenged by rapid decision-making

[592] This means that collaborative thinking often becomes an operational exercise rather than a strategic means of ensuring more effective policy implementation

[593] Foreign policy must be conceived in the broadest possible sense, so that it is the policy's ultimate goal that determines how tasks are solved

[594] Danish efforts are already characterized by holistic thinking in the sense that they typically include a broad range of instruments

[595] To put it bluntly, it is typically a "staple approach", where several instruments come into play simultaneously, but without deep coordination between the individual instruments

[596] The concept of 'joint thinking' is often associated with civil-military joint thinking

[597] But integrated thinking should be understood more broadly and across individual policy areas: Firstly, foreign policy must be integrated across the board, i.e. across the relevant ministries and authorities

[598] Regardless of whether it is within one ministerial area or between several ministerial areas, common goals must guide the task

[599] This requires that there is a common understanding of the nature of the tasks and the objectives and rationale behind them

[600] Secondly, integrated thinking must take place in depth, so that there is coherence between the highest decision-making levels and the implementing levels on the ground

[601] And this connection goes both ways, so that the implementing agencies are aware of the overall objectives, and the decision-makers are aware of the reality in which the decisions must be implemented

[602] Thirdly, not only the central administration, but also other parts of society must be involved in solving the task

[603] Collaborative thinking is not just a government task but a way of thinking where the entire society should be seen as a resource base

[604] This means that, for example, universities, businesses, pension funds, civil society and cities can be actors in a coherent foreign policy

[605] Finally, foreign policy must be integrated in relation to foreign actors

[606] This applies to international organizations, states and private partners

[607] If Denmark and other countries are to have the greatest possible effect from their efforts, they must be coordinated and organized so that the effect is increased and unnecessary duplication is avoided

[608] Strategic and long-term division of labor between partners

[609] is becoming a more important framework condition in light of scarce resources and growing challenges

[610] Global development towards

[611] Chapter 2 uncovers the foreign policy trends that are predicted to have the greatest impact on Denmark's interests up to

[612] The analysis is based on extensive data material, including economic and demographic analyses prepared by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and a 2030 trend analysis from the Danish Defence Intelligence Service

[613] The individual topics and developments have also been discussed in detail with Danish and foreign experts

[614] The international community has made great progress over recent decades towards a more prosperous, peaceful and stable world

[615] In many places, things are going well historically

[616] Since 1990, the number of extremely poor people has more than halved, and the global middle class has tripled

[617] Significant progress has been made in the fight against infectious diseases

[618] The number of children out of primary school has almost halved

[619] More countries are integrating into the global economy

[620] The spread of the Internet, mobile telephony and other technological advances is providing new economic opportunities for millions of people

[621] Many of these positive developments are expected to continue and in some areas accelerate towards

[622] However, progress has not been evenly distributed around the world, and the global community continues to face significant challenges

[623] Persistent or resurgent conflicts hinder economic development in some of the world's vulnerable countries and regions

[624] Likewise, fragility, weak governance, a historically high number of displaced people, pandemics, climate change and resource scarcity can amplify existing conflict lines and challenges

[625] In general, economic, political and societal developments are becoming increasingly unpredictable

[626] This means stricter requirements in the form of a flexible foreign and security policy

[627] It also sets new frameworks for the relationship between state and citizen

[628] Increased unpredictability means that any analysis of foreign policy developments in a 10-15 year perspective is inherently fraught with uncertainty

[629] However, a number of key development trends can be identified

[630] Europe at a crossroads Over recent decades, Denmark and the EU have benefited from a rules-based and liberal international order and a relatively peaceful and stable security policy landscape in Europe

[631] In the next 10-15 years, however, Denmark will have to navigate a European and global context that will differ significantly in several ways from the post-Cold War era

[632] and the other EU countries are facing a new landscape of challenges and threats

[633] The Russia-Ukraine conflict, ISIL's attempts to establish a caliphate in Syria and Iraq, and massive refugee and migration flows challenge EU cooperation and have, among other things, put free movement under pressure

[634] Added to this is the financial crisis and continued economic slowdown in Europe

[635] What all these challenges have in common is that they either unfold within the EU or close to its borders and have direct, visible and noticeable consequences for the security, prosperity and values of Europeans

[636] This has put the cohesion force under considerable pressure

[637] The British referendum on continued EU membership thus takes place at a time when the EU is at a crossroads in many ways, and where there is also growing Euroscepticism and nationalism in several other countries. Taken together, these challenges pose a significant risk that an already inward-looking EU will become even more closed off in the coming years

[638] So far, European countries have – despite disagreements – shown a clear interest in maintaining the institutions and cooperation procedures that have taken many decades to build and which have provided economic growth, stability and prosperity

[639] A stable and prosperous EU is in Denmark's clear economic interest, not least through the internal market, where studies show that Denmark is one of the countries that achieves the absolute greatest gains

[640] Denmark also conducts its trade policy through the EU, which gives it increased weight and influence on the global stage and the opportunity for new free trade agreements with, among others, Asian emerging economies and the United States

[641] The future of the EU will be shaped at the intersection of economic and political pressure for greater integration on the one hand, and national movements against the surrender of sovereignty on the other

[642] The EU's challenge is that political legitimacy is strongly linked to the nation-state, while effective solutions are linked to policies at the European level

[643] This contradiction is expected to continue to lead to cooperation at different speeds, with a core of countries establishing more in-depth cooperation while other countries remain on the periphery

[644] In such a situation, progress in cooperation will require that the core countries achieve a more efficient decision-making process, but that there is sufficient flexibility for the union to accommodate both core and peripheral countries

[645] European security order under pressure In recent decades, Europe has managed security, stability and common norms through multilateral cooperation in the EU, NATO, OSCE and the Council of Europe

[646] The transatlantic alliance has been the primary guarantor of security in Europe, while the EU has tied countries' interests together through economic and political integration and brought prosperity and peaceful coexistence between EU member states

[647] The absence of direct military threats since the fall of the Wall has given Europe a window to extend security and prosperity eastward, and the enlargements of the EU and NATO have concretely increased the European space of free, democratic societies

[648] Russia's illegal annexation of Crimea and intervention in eastern Ukraine have violated central principles of the European and international security order

[649] Russia's military offensive in Syria has also given a new dimension to the country's international engagement

[650] The picture also includes the fact that Russia is undergoing a comprehensive modernization of its armed forces and is apparently also lowering the threshold for using its nuclear military capabilities

[651] Domestically, Russia is moving in a more authoritarian direction and breaking with the notion of a Russia that will eventually move towards a liberal democracy

[652] Russia is therefore expected to continue to be an autocratic state with great power ambitions in

[653] From a Russian perspective, it is Russia that is under pressure from the West, which is trying to maintain its dominant role on the international stage

[654] According to the Russian National Security Strategy, it is necessary to strengthen Russia due to new threats to the country's national security

[655] At the same time, the Russian economy

[656] an Achilles heel for the country

[657] The recession in Russia is increasing pressure on financial reserves, and the country's ability to finance a continued budget deficit could be exhausted in a relatively short time, especially with a persistently low global oil price

[658] Despite threatening statements and exercise activities, Russia hardly represents a direct threat to Denmark's territory, but Russian activities nevertheless constitute a significant foreign and security policy challenge

[659] The end of the Cold War opened a window for mutually beneficial economic and political cooperation between Russia and the EU, which has now closed again

[660] The introduction of mutual sanctions between the EU and Russia and the partial political isolation of Russia – for example, by suspending Russian participation in, among others, the G8/G7 – has limited trade and foreign policy dialogue

[661] As part of a balanced foreign policy approach, the EU and the US have, however, maintained active engagement in a number of multilateral forums where Russia is at the table

[662] The OSCE handles issues of regional stability and security, including significant parts of the crisis in Ukraine, while the Council of Europe provides a framework for often difficult discussions about compliance with common values ​​such as freedom of expression and the media, gender equality and the protection of minorities

[663] Since Russia became a member in 2012, the WTO has provided a framework for dispute settlement cases brought by the EU against Russia

[664] The Baltic Sea Council and the Arctic Council are maintained as channels of dialogue to avoid the Ukraine crisis having a negative spillover effect on cooperation in other areas, including the Arctic

[665] The Russian military intervention in Ukraine is part of a demonstration of power that is being carried out with a wide range of instruments, including those that are purely military: from economic sanctions to cyberattacks to subversive intelligence activities and an extensive propaganda effort, including against Russians inside and outside Russia

[666] This behavior calls into question the post-Fall vision of a cooperative and democratic Europe without dividing lines, but also basic principles of state sovereignty, territorial integrity, and free choice of alliances

[667] It can thus challenge Europe's overall security architecture. Conflicts, fragility and extremism Together with Europe's eastern neighbours, the southern neighbours in the Middle East and North Africa are increasingly drawing an arc of crisis and insecurity that stretches from the northeast to the southwest

[668] With the prospect of continued conflicts, civil wars and transnational militant extremism, the Middle East and North Africa, as well as the broader Sahel region and the Horn of Africa, are likely to be a significant source of instability in the years ahead

[669] This has direct effects for Europe and Denmark

[670] The economies of the Middle Eastern states are largely based on oil or external financial support and to a lesser extent on productivity in the societies

[671] The regimes' revenues only come from tax collection to a small extent, and those in power do not prioritize economic growth in civil society

[672] This means an absence of strong private sectors that can challenge state sectors, demand strengthened rule of law principles, and create jobs

[673] High population growth and high unemployment require significant economic growth in order not to erode living standards, and in most countries there is no immediate prospect of the extensive economic and social reforms necessary for such growth

[674] At the same time, the Middle Eastern economies are being integrated into the global economy, which will highlight the lack of development and put further pressure on the regimes

[675] Technological developments mean increasingly open societies, which make it difficult for states to restrict information flows

[676] As populations see what conditions are like elsewhere, it increases the pressure from below for change, as the Arab Spring also expressed

[677] There is potential for positive development in the region in light of a large youth generation and a relatively well-educated population, and at times a sense of hope and entrepreneurial drive

[678] But economic development requires comprehensive reforms

[679] The most likely scenario in the medium term is continued conflict and stagnation

[680] A complex geopolitical game is taking place between the major powers in the region, which has so far contributed to exacerbating the conflicts

[681] One of the main elements is a rivalry between Sunni and Shiite Muslim states and groups, with Iran and Saudi Arabia in the leading roles

[682] In reality, this is a power struggle for regional dominance, in which religious and ethnic differences are simply included, and it can mean further fragmentation and weakening of the cohesion of states

[683] The regional chaos has contributed to the rise of ISIL, which seeks to conquer territories and establish a caliphate that challenges existing state structures

[684] ISIL's extensive and professional propaganda contributes to the radicalization of young Muslims in the region, but also in Europe

[685] A significant number of Danes and Europeans have traveled to Iraq and Syria, where they receive weapons training, combat experience and become further radicalized

[686] Terrorist attacks in Paris, Brussels, Ankara, Copenhagen and elsewhere have exposed the difficulties of combating terrorism

[687] ISIL has largely taken over the militant Islamist agenda from al-Qaeda, both radicalizing it and strengthening its spread

[688] Regardless of the outcome of the current fight against ISIL in Iraq and Syria, and regardless of whether the group survives in its current form, ISIL has energized a unifying movement that attracts other extremist terrorist groups from Afghanistan in the east to the Sahel region in the west and with offshoots in Europe, among other places

[689] Regardless of its future form, this movement can be expected to be a driving force for extremism and terrorism for a number of years to come, both in Europe's southern regions and in Europe

[690] The conflicts in the Middle East, North Africa and other parts of Africa and Central Asia will continue to create refugee flows

[691] Although a large number of refugees will seek Europe, the vast majority – similar to the world's current approximately 60 million displaced people – will reside in the immediate areas close to the conflicts

[692] This puts already fragile regions under pressure and creates the risk of social, cultural, political and economic tensions between refugees and local communities

[693] At the same time, displaced people today spend much longer in refugee camps and other temporary settlements

[694] The average number of years displaced is up to 20 years today, partly because the conflicts have become more protracted

[695] And the longer people are away from their homes, the harder it becomes to return

[696] The melting of the ice opens up the Arctic. The Kingdom of Denmark is a great power in the Arctic context

[697] And with the gradual melting of the ice, the Kingdom becomes the center of a unique development, where the world, for the first time in centuries, is truly expanding with new land and new sea areas

[698] The Arctic is gradually being integrated with the rest of the world, and development in the high north will no longer take place in isolation

[699] Perspectives will open up for increased economic activity in the form of, for example, fishing, research, raw material extraction, maritime transport and tourism, and other forms of development for the benefit of local populations

[700] And with that also come political opportunities for increased international cooperation to the benefit of both Greenland and the rest of the Kingdom

[701] But not all parts of the development will proceed at the same speed, and low raw material prices and high establishment costs, among other things, have so far limited the extraction of raw materials

[702] The new geopolitical picture in the Arctic is only just beginning to take shape

[703] With gradually increased activity in the Arctic, there will be more international focus

[704] In this light, the Kingdom, as a significant Arctic power, will have a major responsibility for managing and ensuring peaceful regional development through active foreign policy efforts

[705] Not only in the Arctic, but also in relation to the EU and those states outside the Arctic region that are increasing their Arctic focus

[706] With the so-called Ilulissat Declaration from 2008, the five Arctic coastal states committed themselves to acting responsibly in the Arctic and to resolving disagreements through negotiations

[707] But Russia's unpredictable behavior can also affect the security situation in the Arctic

[708] It is unlikely that this will lead to direct military conflicts, but it emphasizes that Denmark and the other coastal states may risk having to deal with the security consequences of increased political and military tension in the region and in Europe

[709] Ultimately, the security of the entire Kingdom is guaranteed through NATO membership, including in the Arctic

[710] A further political uncertainty is linked to the Arctic states' overlapping claims to Arctic sea areas

[711] It is likely that Denmark and Russia from the UN

[712] both will receive support for the overlapping claims on the Arctic seabed, and that therefore a final border demarcation must be negotiated

[713] Such a negotiation process could be protracted and accompanied by Russian pressure on the Kingdom, including through military deployments

[714] Russia is fundamentally considered to be interested in stable political development in the region, but the generally reduced international trust in Russia has meant that Russian military activity in the Arctic is followed with skepticism

[715] However, the increasing Russian military presence and activity in the Arctic can to some extent be justified by an increased need for civil preparedness and maintaining the strategic balance with the United States

[716] The economic center of gravity is shifting eastward

[717] Developments in the world economy in recent decades have been characterized by very strong economic growth in Asia, and in particular in China

[718] It has gradually shifted the global political and economic center of gravity from west to east

[719] This development will continue in the period up to

[720] Around 85% of global growth in the coming years is expected to take place outside Europe, with more than half of this in the Asia-Pacific region

[721] Among the leading global growth countries, China is predicted to account for 30% of global growth, while the United States will account for 15%

[722] Even with slightly lower growth rates, China is expected to ▪

[723] Increased trade in global value chains, where companies split production into a chain of sub-activities that are carried out in different countries and add value to the product

[724] Significant increase in trade flows

[725] including Asia

[726] In about 10 years, total trade in goods and services in Asia is expected to surpass internal trade in Europe, which today constitutes the world's largest trading bloc

[727] Increased integration of developing countries in global trade, with particular emphasis on the G20 developing countries, including not least China

[728] Increased trade with China is the main driving force behind increasing South-South trade, and weaker growth in Chinese trade will thus constitute a risk element for other developing countries

[729] Growth in trade in services, which is globally dominated by the richer and developed countries, which account for approximately two-thirds of trade
