[733] Despite a European population growth of approximately 200 million over the past 65 years, Europe's share of the world's population has fallen from 22% in 1950 to 10% in

[734] This is due to the strong population growth in other regions – especially in Asia, but also in Africa

[735] Demographic shifts will continue until

[736] The world population will reach approximately 8.5 billion in 2030, and Asia's population will be almost seven times that of Europe

[737] With almost one and a half billion people, India will overtake China as the world's most populous nation

[738] This will mean 170 million more Indians of working age, while China will experience the largest absolute decline in the workforce, with around 45 million people

[739] Among the BRIC countries, however, Russia will experience the largest relative decline

[740] Africa will grow by about 40% from just under 1 billion today to about 1.4 billion people in 2030, while the Middle East and North Africa will grow by 25% or about 125 million

[741] Nigeria alone will experience population growth equivalent to the entire population of Germany over the next 15 years

[742] Conversely, the European population will experience a natural decline of approximately 5 million, and this development will increase further in the following decades

[743] While the world's population is generally aging, regions will be characterized by large differences in age composition

[744] In 2030, the median age in Europe will be 45 years, while in North Africa it will be 28 years

[745] Europe and East Asia will experience slightly declining labor forces, while Africa will experience the largest increase in the number of people of working age (15-64 years

[746] Despite the current European unemployment rate of around 10%, Europe may face a shortage of qualified workers in the coming years

[747] Free movement within the EU has meant that countries like Denmark have attracted labor, especially from Eastern and Central European countries

[748] As the supply of European labor is depleted, there may be a need for labor from countries outside Europe

[749] How the declining workforce will affect economic growth will depend, among other things, on productivity and technological development

[750] But a shrinking workforce and increased dependency ratios will, all else being equal, put pressure on economic growth and public finances. Conversely, countries with large, young populations have the opportunity to benefit from a demographic surplus, where a large workforce and relatively fewer children and elderly people result in a lower dependency ratio

[751] But this requires job opportunities for the many millions of young people who enter the labor market every year

[752] The ability to ensure sufficiently high growth and job opportunities for millions of young people will have a major impact on social stability, mobility and migration, especially in Africa and the Middle East

[753] The next 10-15 years will thus be characterized by both “pull” and “push” factors for international migration

[754] “Pull” factors in the form of aging and labor shortages, especially in Europe

[755] “Push” factors in the form of high unemployment and lack of economic prospects in regions characterized by poverty, conflict and climate change

[756] At the same time, the spread of internet access and smartphones will contribute to making global inequalities in living conditions visible

[757] Deeper globalization, where, in line with the strengthened value chains in global production and technological development, there will be a need to intensify global cooperation and regulations in a number of trade policy areas

[758] Economic growth, and not least the development in China and India, which has lifted 700 million out of poverty, has contributed to decreasing global inequality

[759] However, there is a tendency for inequality within countries to grow, which, according to the OECD and IMF, challenges both economic growth and social cohesion

[760] The ability of political systems to ensure growth and handle popular pressure, especially when crises arise, becomes crucial to their stability

[761] China's great importance to the global economy is both an opportunity and a risk factor

[762] The transition of China's economy from being export and investment-driven to being driven more by private consumption will lead to lower economic growth

[763] The question is whether Chinese growth will gradually reach a new level, or whether there will be a more significant slowdown in the economy, possibly coupled with a crisis in the financial sector

[764] A prolonged economic crisis in China could have a significant impact on the global economy

[765] Chinese developments are not only important for the country's own socio-economic development, but also for other countries, which have become more dependent on China over a number of years

[766] This could challenge the massive poverty eradication of recent decades and increase the risk that new members of the middle class will fall back into poverty

[767] At the same time, rising debt burdens in many emerging economies, combined with continued low commodity prices and possible interest rate increases, could increase pressure on national budgets and constitute a source of economic and political instability

[768] Population growth creates fertile ground for migration In recent decades, there has been a significant shift in the world's population from developed countries to developing countries

[775] The big cities will feel many of the global challenges most clearly: urban pockets of poverty, inequality, pollution, water shortages, inadequate waste solutions and infrastructure problems

[776] As the largest cities grow and become more densely populated, access to clean drinking water and sanitation, as well as the need for public goods such as education and healthcare, will increase

[777] The increasing population density also creates favorable conditions for the spread of infectious diseases and, together with increased mobility between countries and continents, also for pandemics

[778] The Ebola outbreak in West Africa in particular has created renewed focus on combating pandemics

[779] The ability to respond quickly and effectively to future outbreaks will depend on national and international crisis response structures

[780] Rapid urbanization is making cities new economic and political power centers in terms of economic activity, political influence, and international attractiveness

[781] In parallel, the world's leading cities are expected to become more self-aware political and economic actors in the international arena. Cities and provinces have already shown themselves to be more ambitious than nation states in several areas, including the climate

[782] City networks like C40 have become an important tool for mayors and governors to exchange experiences, share solutions to common challenges, and influence development at the regional and global levels

[783] Climate change and energy production

[784] Climate change is increasingly seen as a threat multiplier that will contribute to instability, fragility and migration

[785] According to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, climate change will exacerbate existing resource challenges such as access to water and thus also food production

[786] The demand for water will increase by 40-50% by 2030, and the number of people living with severe water shortages is predicted to have doubled by 2030. The Middle East and North Africa are among the regions that will be most negatively affected by climate change

[787] The region is home to 7% of the world's population, but has only 1.5% of the world's drinking water

[788] Parts of the region are already facing acute water shortages as a result of one of the worst and longest droughts ever, and climate change is expected to exacerbate the situation

[792] The climate agreement at COP21 in Paris in December 2015 was the culmination of many years of negotiations on a new course in the fight against climate change

[793] The agreement commits all countries – developed and developing countries alike – to intensify the fight against climate change

[794] COP21 also recognized the great importance of businesses, investors, cities, provinces and other non-state actors in climate action

[795] Both cities and private foundations have declared their readiness to join governments in bringing new financing and technology into the climate fight, including through investments in clean energy

[796] As a result of economic and demographic growth, global energy demand is expected to increase by approximately 30% by 2030, although technological advances and efficiency measures are expected to almost halve the correlation between economic growth and energy consumption

[797] Up to 90 percent of the increasing demand is predicted to come from developing countries and emerging economies

[798] A large part will continue to be covered by oil, coal and gas, but alternative energy sources such as nuclear power, solar, wind and biomass will play a greater role

[799] According to the International Energy Agency, investments in the global energy sector over the next 25 years amount to 68 trillion USD

[800] It is estimated that around a quarter of the investment volume can be expected in areas where Denmark has strong competencies and companies, namely energy efficiency in buildings and industry, renewable energy in power supply and biofuels

[801] At the same time, new technology such as fracking’ with the extraction of shale gas and oil has

[802] changed the global energy market

[804] New extraction opportunities will also mitigate the risk of drastic increases in oil prices

[805] The long-term development in the global energy market will increase the pressure for reform on countries such as Saudi Arabia, Russia, Venezuela and Nigeria, whose economies and state finances are currently mainly based on the export of oil and gas

[806] Technologically interconnected societies Innovation and the spread of new technologies are increasing exponentially in speed and are fundamentally changing markets, forms of communication and workflows

[807] By 2030, the Internet is expected to have spread to over half of the world's population, connecting millions of people, including in the world's poorest regions, to the global network

[808] It will make the world even more interconnected

[809] And it will provide new economic opportunities and social benefits through access to data in health, education and many other areas

[810] The rapid digitalization, internet-connected components and automation of markets and societies – the so-called fourth industrial revolution – will change global trade, production methods and the workplaces of the future

[811] New technologies such as 3D printing, mobile and cloud technology, artificial intelligence and robotics, healthcare and biotechnology are leading to demographic and socio-economic changes

[812] In the short term, this will mean that certain types of jobs will disappear

[813] But the development will also create new sectors and job types

[814] Overall, the development will place great demands on the restructuring and further training of the workforce and the internationalization of companies

[815] The comparative advantage of low-wage labor will become less important, and future production will be able to take place closer to the consumer and tailored to individual needs and preferences to a greater extent than before

[816] This could mean a return of manufacturing jobs to developed countries due to their technological and educational level

[817] This development also entails the risk of new forms of crime, surveillance and violation of individual privacy

[818] Cyber threats encompass a wide range of activities from state-based espionage targeting authorities, to industrial espionage, to propaganda and the spread of misinformation and attacks on private individuals

[819] The cyber threats that pose a strategic and security policy challenge are primarily the state-led build-up of capacity to spy on states and large companies or to potentially carry out devastating attacks against important societal functions

[820] Towards a new international order The international system has generally shown great stability and robustness since the Second World War

[821] Multilateral diplomacy has helped prevent direct armed conflict between great powers

[822] The number of wars between countries has been historically low

[823] At the same time, the peaceful rise of China and India has so far largely taken place within existing international structures

[824] Economic growth, growing interdependence, social progress, and an increasingly branched network of international organizations will continue to increase the incentive for cooperation and mitigate the risk of conflict between states

[825] However, the increasing dispersion of power can also lead to periods of unrest, geopolitical competition and the risk of conflict until the global balance of power between the great powers has found a new footing

[826] The stability of the international system will largely depend on the relationship between the US and China, while the EU and strong states such as India, Brazil, Russia and a number of other countries will assume a significant international role

[827] Despite the EU's economic weight, the notion of a global balance of power based on the US, China and the EU in a 'G3' seems most likely to be replaced by a 'G2', where the relationship between the US and China in particular will be important for the stability of a more multipolar system

[828] The United States will maintain its leading position in global security policy until

[829] No likely combination of countries will

[830] could match the extraordinary power and alliance system of the United States

[831] The combined economic, military, political and cultural strength of the United States and Europe can continue to have a stabilizing influence on the international order until

[832] The transatlantic relationship is fueled by close economic, value-based and cultural ties

[833] This alliance becomes even stronger if ties to India, Japan and other Asian democracies are taken into account

[834] China will be the world's largest economy by

[835] The country will continue to dominate Asia economically, and its foreign policy towards neighboring countries is expected to be characterized by increased assertiveness

[836] In addition, China will increasingly exploit close partnerships with countries in Asia, Africa and Latin America

[837] China is expected to strengthen its engagement in multilateral cooperation structures, particularly in the UN and regionally, including with ASEAN and in APEC and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation

[838] The new Chinese-led Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) could gain a significant place among the other multilateral development banks

[839] However, in 2030, China will still not be able to match the United States militarily and will primarily focus on strategic stability and open trade relations

[840] The Lisbon Treaty has given the EU

[841] the institutional prerequisites for being able to play a larger and more streamlined global role

[842] But the EU continues to have difficulty translating its global economic weight into foreign policy impact

[843] The EU's international influence unfolds in an interaction between the common foreign and security policy and the individual foreign policies of the 28 member states, with the UK, France and increasingly Germany at the forefront

[844] The EU is at the table in dealing with most global challenges, but typically does not have a leading role

[845] However, there are areas where the EU has gained a stronger international voice

[846] The adoption of EU sanctions was instrumental in bringing Iran to the negotiating table, just as EU sanctions have supported German-French efforts to resolve the conflict between Russia and Ukraine

[847] In light of the changing threat landscape in Europe, security and defense policy cooperation is expected to receive increased focus in the EU's new Global Strategy, which will be launched in the summer of 2016. The continued shift in economic growth will translate into a desire from new, strong states to have greater influence on international political and economic decisions and the framework within which decisions are made

[848] At the same time, an increasing number of challenges will exceed the capabilities of states and demand new and broader societal alliances

[849] Non-state actors such as cities, provinces, multinational corporations, foundations, informal groups and powerful individuals will gain increased global influence

[850] A wider range of actors will therefore want a seat at the table when international decisions are made

[851] Globalization has thus accelerated a dispersion of power, where states no longer have a monopoly on foreign and security policy

[852] National governments and international institutions will increasingly find that there will be developments that they cannot predict and have no control over

[853] In that situation, effective international responses will depend on the strength and breadth of international and societal partnerships

[854] In a more diverse world with more powerful actors, it will be crucial to maintain a rules-based international order that states that are moving up the international hierarchy see as legitimate and accept and act in, and in which other countries can also recognize themselves

[855] The effectiveness of international cooperation is currently limited by a lack of reform of the primary multilateral institutions

[856] The UN, the World Bank and the IMF in particular will have to adapt to the increased dispersion of power in order not to lose relevance or support

[857] The composition of the UN Security Council largely reflects the balance of power at the end of World War II, and mutual distrust and veto power mean that the lowest common denominator often wins

[858] Lack of reforms can also be met with the establishment of alternative and perhaps overlapping institutions and structures or the strengthening of informal forums such as the G7 and G

[859] However, multilateral diplomacy has delivered a number of significant results in 2015: the UN's adoption of the 2030 Agenda in New York and the agreements on development financing in Addis Ababa and climate change in Paris

[860] Similarly, the agreement in Nairobi on a package of free trade reforms has signaled a possible way forward for the WTO

[861] The new development agenda with 17 global goals is a showdown with the traditional divisions between “rich” and “poor” countries and between North and South with a universal agenda that commits all countries in the world to the same goals

[862] The agreements underscore the demand for global solutions and give renewed momentum to multilateral cooperation

[863] There are also other signs that the new, powerful players are increasing their engagement in multilateral organizations and funds

[864] For example, China is expected to play an increased role in maintaining international order and stability, including through contributions to UN peacekeeping forces

[865] The future strength of international organizations will therefore depend on the ability to ensure a dynamic in which the voice of China and other major developing countries is increased

[866] The development will have an impact on the norms, values and principles that have been considered by the West as fixed components of the international system, but which are not necessarily shared by the major growth and developing countries

[867] Denmark, the EU and other Western nations will in future have to conduct foreign policy in a context where liberal, democratic principles and the Western social model are not seen as given, let alone as attractive, in the same way as before

[868] On the contrary, Western principles and positions are increasingly being challenged, including with a greater focus on collective rights and social harmony rather than individually based rights

[869] Growing distances in positions in

[870] including the UN

[871] Human Rights Councils are likely to pose an increasing challenge in the coming years

[872] The notion that countries will almost automatically move in a more democratic direction as income levels increase has not always been proven to be true

[873] Some experts instead speak of a real recession for democracy and human rights

[874] Within the EU, too, there is a movement towards increased nationalism and, in some countries, pressure on freedoms, which could in the long term significantly weaken Europe's own credibility and influence when it comes to upholding value-based norms and rights internationally

[875] Overall, Denmark is facing a new foreign policy reality characterized by political and economic power shifts, a heightened security situation, and a more technologically connected and unpredictable world, which is increasingly characterized by new actors with global ambitions

[876] These developments will set the framework for Danish foreign and security policy in the next 10-15 years

[877] It places demands on the safeguarding of the Kingdom's interests, security and values

[878] But it also creates new opportunities to promote the welfare of the population

[879] The Foreign Service's task performance

[880] The Foreign Service's current framework describes the current and future requirements for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs' performance of its tasks

[881] The chapter highlights perspectives for the future foreign service as the international link for the entire Danish society

[882] The changing global context

[883] Reductions in the Foreign Service's operating budget create a need to rethink, prioritize and focus Denmark's future representation of interests

[884] The Foreign Service has the overall responsibility for organizing and coordinating Denmark's relations abroad in close cooperation with the Ministry of Defense and a number of other ministries and authorities

[885] In a globalized and interconnected world, the fundamental purposes of diplomacy will remain the same

[886] But the instruments must be adapted as the topics become more diverse and interconnected and new actors enter the scene

[887] At the same time, the resource situation exacerbates the need for clear prioritization both in the ministry and at the Danish embassies

[888] The Danish Foreign Service, headed by the Minister of Foreign Affairs, has overall responsibility for the implementation of the government's foreign policy

[889] According to the Foreign Affairs Act of 1983, the purpose of the Foreign Service is to handle the Kingdom's international affairs

[890] The Foreign Service is responsible for and coordinates foreign policy and foreign economic relations abroad, including Denmark's participation in the EU, international organizations, international development cooperation and the handling of international law issues

[891] The Foreign Service must also provide assistance to Danish citizens abroad and to Danish companies in their business relations abroad

[892] The Foreign Service consists of the Ministry in Copenhagen (the Home Service) and Denmark's network of representations abroad (the Foreign Service

[893] The Foreign Service constitutes a joint service and is one authority

[894] The legal basis for Denmark's development cooperation and export promotion efforts is further defined in the Act on International Development Cooperation and the Act on Certain Aspects of the Work of the Trade Council

[895] The Constitution states that it is the government that conducts the country's foreign policy, but that the government has a duty to consult with the Folketing, in particular the Foreign Policy Committee, in matters of greater importance for Denmark's foreign policy

[896] Danish foreign policy has traditionally been characterized by relatively broad political support across the middle in the Folketing, which contributes to continuity in Danish priorities and key issues between changing governments

[897] It is essential to ensure dynamic coordination between the Folketing and the government, for example in connection with visits abroad and network building, so that the entire political Denmark is included as a strategic resource in the planning and implementation of foreign policy

[898] It is a Danish strength that diplomacy, development assistance, trade policy and public export and investment promotion are all concentrated in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs

[899] This provides unique opportunities to exploit the interaction between the various foreign policy instruments, including the involvement of Danish companies' and authorities' expertise and positions of strength in development cooperation

[900] The conditions of globalization and new trends

[901] Since the Fall of the Wall, Danish foreign policy has been particularly directed towards the economic and political consequences of globalization as well as the opportunity to contribute to peace, stability and the spread of human rights globally

[902] The primary purpose has been to minimize the negative consequences and maximize the benefits of a more interconnected world

[903] The Ministry of Foreign Affairs' Globalization Analysis from

[904] The Borderless World has formed the framework for the Foreign Service's adaptation over the past ten years

[905] Denmark's engagement in the hot spots of globalization has been strengthened, including in the growth markets in Asia

[906] Closer cooperation with other Danish authorities has also been established, work on economic diplomacy has been significantly strengthened, and the embassies are contributing more actively to network building across the full range of Danish interests

[907] Developments since 2006 have thus largely confirmed

[908] predictions of globalization analysis and in some areas even surpassed them

[909] This includes the rapid spread of information technology and social media to all parts of the world, as well as the increasing importance of non-state actors with global ambitions – both positively (civil society, charitable foundations, etc.) and negatively (ISIL

[910] This also applies to the interest in Denmark in international affairs, which has, among other things, meant significantly more travelling Danish delegations, ranging from ministerial visits and parliamentary committee trips to business delegations and visits from educational institutions

[911] These visits are largely organized by the Danish representations

[912] An example is the Danish Parliament's committees, whose travel activity has tripled on average in the past five years compared to the early 2000s

[913] The interest in foreign countries is also reflected in the importance of citizen services and preparedness, where the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, for example, assists approximately 5,000 needy Danes annually

[914] The Ministry of Foreign Affairs' website maintains 50 travel guides for Danish travelers, and the website was visited over 1.3 million times in

[915] At the same time, new global trends of importance to Denmark are being seen

[916] The melting of the ice and developments in the Arctic region create a need for significantly greater Danish efforts

[917] The security policy climate in Europe and its neighboring areas to the east and south has deteriorated and necessitates new prioritization and a refocusing on security policy

[918] The development has thus not weakened the need to handle the traditional core diplomatic tasks. Quite the contrary

[919] The maintenance of the foreign and security policy agendas is central to efforts in other areas, including economic diplomacy

[920] Furthermore, the global economic crisis since 2008 has challenged small open economies like Denmark with tendencies towards global protectionism and decisions made in informal forums such as the G

[921] In the EU, the prolonged economic crisis management has eroded the ability to deliver effective, pan-European responses to crises, not least the current refugee and migration crisis

[922] Overall, these developments lead to stricter requirements for Denmark's representation of interests both regionally and globally in the coming years

[925] Grants, representations and employees

[926] At the same time, significant savings have been made in the public sector in Denmark, which has also affected the resources for international tasks in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and other ministries

[927] The Ministry of Foreign Affairs' overall area of responsibility has remained the same since 2000, when the state's export and investment promotion was consolidated into a new organization, the Danish Trade Council, under the Ministry of Foreign Affairs

[928] From 2000 to 2016, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs' grant

[929] for the operation of the entire group has decreased by 600 million

[930] According to the Finance Act for 2016, the appropriation is expected to decrease by a further approximately DKK 160 million towards

[931] This will result in an overall decrease in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs' operating budget of almost DKK 800 million or 33% since

[932] The savings in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs have been implemented through various initiatives

[933] Firstly, digitalization has enabled ongoing efficiency improvements and rationalizations of operations and workflows, including between the ministry in Copenhagen and the embassies

[934] Secondly, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs has on several occasions implemented major organizational changes and deprioritized tasks

[935] Most recently, in connection with the 2016 Finance Act, a decision was made to close down five offices and completely or partially deprioritized a number of policy areas and specific tasks in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs

[936] These adjustments will contribute to meeting the requirement to close approximately 200 positions in the field and home service over the coming years

[937] Thirdly, there has been an adjustment of the foreign service's representations and staff composition

[938] Since 2000, the number of representations with seconded staff has decreased by approximately 20% from 120 to 95, mainly as a result of consolidation and rationalization of separate trade offices following the establishment of the Danish Trade Council in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs

[939] The number of embassies has fluctuated since the turn of the millennium and currently stands at 71 embassies

[940] In terms of personnel, the ministry employed approximately 2,500 employees in 2015, divided into approximately 800 at the ministry in Copenhagen and 1,700 at the representations

[941] Since 2000, there has been a significant shift towards a larger proportion of local employees (i.e. Danes and foreigners employed and paid directly by the embassies) from approximately 35% to over half of the staff in

[942] The proportion of employees at Asiatisk Plads and those posted at the representations has thus fallen from approximately 65% in 2000 to approximately 45% in 2011. The job cuts in the field and home service over the coming years will be a continuation of this trend

[943] A recent survey has shown that Denmark – apart from Iceland – currently has the smallest foreign service among the Nordic countries. If Denmark is to maintain strong influence in the areas that matter most, there is therefore a need for sharp prioritization and deprioritization of tasks

[944] And the ability to enter into new forms of collaboration, where the ministry, employees and representations carry out tasks in partnership with other stakeholders and actors

[951] Given its great importance for Danish legislation, smooth and effective coordination of Denmark's position on EU issues is a particularly central task for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs as the coordinating authority

[952] An effective domestic EU decision-making process in relation to the Parliament's European Affairs Committee and internally within the government provides increased Danish influence in negotiations in the EU and ensures subsequent implementation and compliance with EU legislation in Denmark

[953] The Ministry of Foreign Affairs must constitute the international link for the entire Danish society

[954] This will ensure strategic focus, so that efforts and resources are prioritized where Denmark has the most at stake and create the best conditions for making a difference - either alone or in partnership with others

[956] The Foreign Service should be the focal point for the protection of Denmark's interests abroad

[957] Through an active and well-thought-out foreign policy, it must help increase domestic political room for manoeuvre and thereby ensure that Danish society can be structured as we wish

[959] A more diverse international arena with both new strong states and non-state actors will, all else being equal, lead to increased competition to set the agenda

[968] Furthermore, experience with Danish domestic political and socio-economic conditions and the work on Slotsholmen are central to representing Danish interests

[969] Local employees can therefore only replace posted employees to a certain extent

[970] In general, it is a challenge for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs that an increasing part of the diplomatic corps does not consider the Ministry of Foreign Affairs as a lifetime employer

[971] While there is a continuous intake of new skilled and highly motivated employees, experience and knowledge are being lost, both in breadth and depth

[972] The requirement for mobility and flexibility is being further challenged in recent years by changed framework conditions in connection with secondments

[973] Overall, there has been a reduction in the financial framework for those deployed, especially in posts in Europe and North America

[974] The changes have been implemented, among other things, on the premise that an accompanying spouse also has work during the posting

[975] However, only half of the accompanying spouses are able to find employment

[976] This means that a large proportion of families face a dilemma in terms of accepting a decrease in income during a multi-year deployment

[977] If the ministry is to continue to be able to recruit and retain the most qualified employees, the conditions for secondees – especially below manager level – should be improved

[978] This ensures that the service will also have the best personnel resources to safeguard Denmark's interests in a 10-15 year perspective

[979] The employees are the Foreign Service's most important resource

[980] The Foreign Service primarily needs employees who possess international experience and outlook, language skills and a high degree of expertise and professionalism

[981] There is a great professional need for generalists who can cover the entire range of foreign policy tasks and are thus able to broadly represent Danish interests, including at the Danish embassies

[982] Competence building typically takes place internally within the Ministry of Foreign Affairs through rotation between different departments and through secondment

[983] But there is also a need for specialists in specific foreign policy priorities that require linguistic, geographical or thematic expertise

[984] This can be met with targeted career paths in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, but also through external recruitment from, for example, think tanks, universities, the private business community or international organizations

[985] In the Netherlands, for example, there is a greater exchange between the foreign service and the think tank environment, which results in better utilization of societal expertise

[986] To increase international experience, it is also possible to benefit from more systematic and targeted use of secondments, where Danish employees are placed in international organizations

[987] A secondment strengthens the individual employee's – and ultimately Denmark's – knowledge and network in international organizations

[988] This also applies to subject areas where there are special foreign and security policy interests at stake

[989] Secondments are already used, but the effort could be strengthened, also in relation to other parts of the central administration (climate, business promotion, etc

[990] A more strategic approach to secondments would require that the existing consultant allocation under development assistance be increased, and that a separate pool could be allocated centrally for cases where development policy cannot be applied

[991] Locally employed employees at Denmark's representations, as the largest staff group, are an important resource for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and a source of local insight, networks and language skills that are used for the benefit of Danish companies and authorities

[992] However, there are a number of competencies that local employees, unlike posted diplomats, cannot immediately be expected to possess

[993] This applies, for example, to broad knowledge of economic diplomacy, development aid, security policy, European policy, and international law and human rights

[994] This also applies to insight into geographical areas of particular importance

[995] The embassies must function as a lookout post for all of Denmark and build solid knowledge about other countries' practices and experiences in areas that are closely linked to Danish interests and values

[996] Mass media and social media lead to an overload of information and data, which embassies in particular must help to sort through and qualify for the benefit of domestic decision-making

[997] The work is done in close collaboration with relevant ministries and authorities, so that the Foreign Service's instruments and capabilities serve the interests of the entire government

[998] The ability of embassies to create results requires a physical presence and the opportunity to build networks and close relationships with politicians, civil servants, business leaders and opinion leaders in the countries in question

[999] Such relationships strengthen the understanding of what is happening in society and create the basis for Denmark to safeguard its interests, including planning fruitful visits for Danish delegations, opening doors for Danish business and assisting Danes in need

[1000] In 2013, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs established an external reflection group to make recommendations for Denmark's future representation structure

[1001] The reflection group concluded, among other things, that Denmark's physical presence is crucial to achieving results and promoting Danish interests

[1002] The group generally recommended “more EU – less Europe” and greater emphasis on the rapidly growing emerging markets

[1003] At the same time, increased focus on economic diplomacy was recommended – but not at the expense of broader foreign and security policy – as well as strengthened integration between development cooperation and opportunities for Danish exports and investments

[1004] It will also be important going forward to continuously review Denmark's representation structure – both the geographical presence and the staffing – in light of the key development trends and long-term Danish foreign and security policy priorities

[1005] As recommended by the reflection group, it should be the foreign policy pursued that drives Denmark's presence, not the other way around

[1006] A logical consequence of this basic principle is also that Denmark must have a sufficiently strong presence in the globally policy-making capitals that are of greatest importance to Danish foreign and security policy interests

[1007] A particular problem is associated with small embassies with 1-2 staff, which constitute 17% of the total number of Danish representations

[1008] Here, the experience is that administrative tasks take up a disproportionately large portion of working time at the expense of core tasks

[1009] The same applies to the use of so called "laptop" ambassadors, who in principle are a single posted diplomat

[1010] Digitalization brings new opportunities for flexible and cost-effective forms of representation

[1011] The following alternatives are particularly mentioned in conversations with Danish stakeholders and foreign partners

[1012] Initiate work that will come up with new ideas and proposals for the foreign service of the future, based, among other things, on experiences and modernization processes in other countries Strengthen cooperation and exchange with think tanks, research environments, business and civil society and increased use of strategic secondments in international organizations Increased regionalization, where regional "mother embassies" take over regular tasks such as administration, citizen services, traditional export promotion, etc. from small embassies (or "laptop" ambassadors), who instead focus resources on building relationships and following local developments Co-location with other countries - e.g. joint Nordic embassies, possibly in connection with Nordic cultural centers Accommodation of a Danish diplomat at another representation, e.g. EU delegation, with the purpose of representing Danish foreign policy interests Private co-financing of embassies - especially in countries where significant Danish business interests are at stake

[1013] Financing can, for example, be done through long-term contracts with the Trade Council or by establishing a fund with a separate board of directors

[1014] Strengthen the analytical basis for foreign policy

[1015] through better use of research and data-based knowledge and systematic involvement of the analysis capacity of other authorities, especially the intelligence services * Improve posting conditions for employees, especially below manager level, possibly through internal reprioritization * Continuously ensure that Denmark is represented with sufficient weight in the places that are most important for Danish interests and global policy formulation

[1016] In those countries where Denmark has chosen not to be present, joint tasks should be left to the EU

[1017] In light of the resource situation, new, flexible forms of representation can also be considered. These alternative forms of representation do not provide the same depth or breadth of diplomatic relations as a Danish embassy

[1259] First, to maintain American commitment to European security, where increased European efforts can give renewed strength to the transatlantic bond and emphasize that Europe and the United States have common goals and are working together to achieve them

[1260] Secondly, to strengthen cooperation on counter-terrorism

[1261] Thirdly, to Strategic interests – international legal order and human rights * To promote the international legal order, human rights and Danish values ​​based on a clearly communicated and predictable value-based profile and positive dialogue with partners * To maintain efforts for universal rights within the UN and the EU * That the EU continues to be a significant value-based actor that leads by example * To strengthen alliances with like-minded and non-Western countries with a focus on the most important value-based and human rights-related issues for Denmark * To strengthen cooperation with business and civil society on sustainable growth, investments and human rights. 32 / chapter 4 / Denmark's strategic interests in a connected world expand economic relations with the USA, which is Denmark's third largest export market

[1262] It will be particularly important for Denmark that progress is made in the work on a transatlantic free trade agreement, the so-called TTIP

[1263] The agreement will ensure increased trade and prosperity on both sides of the Atlantic and at the same time set new standards for other agreements around the world

[1264] The EU and the US have higher standards for, for example, health, environment and sustainability than the rest of the world

[1265] TTIP can thus have a positive impact on Denmark, the EU and globally

[1266] Turkey also constitutes a large growth market close to Denmark

[1267] Furthermore, Turkey has great economic, regional and geopolitical importance for the EU and Denmark, including in relation to handling the situation in the Middle East and North Africa and the migration challenges

[1268] We have a strong interest in influencing Turkey bilaterally and through constructive cooperation through the EU and within NATO. 4.2.2 Russia and Eastern Europe Denmark, together with the rest of the Western world, is confronted with a Russia that is developing inwardly in an increasingly authoritarian direction and is potentially more unstable than before

[1269] Russia's illegal annexation of Crimea and the destabilization of eastern Ukraine are violations of the most fundamental elements of the European security order

[1270] This requires a unified and robust response from European states and the rest of the Western world

[1271] The answer has come, among other things, from the fact that the 28 EU countries have continuously introduced, strengthened or extended sanctions against Russia since March 2014, each time unanimously

[1272] It has also come in the form of joint decisions within NATO to strengthen the alliance and its credibility as a guarantor of a stable and peaceful Europe

[1273] There is a constant need to reaffirm unity and strengthen resilience in the EU and NATO

[1274] Russia seeks to undermine European unity through many channels, as has been seen, for example, by directly supporting right-wing nationalist forces such as the French Front National and inciting Russian minorities in Europe

[1275] A comprehensive Russian disinformation effort could similarly affect decision-making power in the open democratic societies of the EU and NATO

[1276] Efforts through other multilateral forums or bilateral relations can supplement the coordinated initiatives through the EU and NATO

[1277] But the main effort must be made through common ground in the two primary organizations that have generally ensured peace and prosperity in Europe for the past three generations, and which can continue to do so if unity is ensured

[1278] Therefore, Denmark must continue to work to ensure agreement in the EU and NATO on a robust and principled line that maintains political and economic pressure on Russia with a view to achieving a solution to the conflict in Ukraine

[1279] Denmark should, among other things, work to ensure continued agreement in the EU on the policy of non-recognition of the annexation of Crimea and on the sanctions policy linked to Russia's actual actions in Crimea and eastern Ukraine

[1280] Increasing isolation is largely a result of the foreign policy line the country is pursuing and the necessary measures the outside world has taken to put pressure on Russia to change its behavior

[1281] But the domestic policy tightening in recent years against the press, civil society, the opposition and other groups in society and the systematic use of internal and external enemy images have also contributed to Russia becoming more closed off in recent years

[1282] Regardless of the fault or reasons, it is not in Denmark's or Europe's interest for the isolation to continue and the dialogue to dry up

[1283] Russia's size and location mean that Denmark and Europe must also take a sober view of Russia's economic and political importance for developments in Europe and Europe's immediate region

[1284] Russia is also a significant market for European products, despite sanctions

[1285] This is an example of a dilemma between commercial interests and values ​​and principles

[1286] Russia is a central player in handling a number of foreign and security policy issues, where it is in the interest of Europe and Denmark to have Russia on board to establish lasting solutions in the Arctic, to crises in the Middle East, to cross-border challenges such as international terrorism and migration, and also to the crises of which Russia itself is a part

[1287] Denmark’s and Europe's identification and maintenance of the common interests and areas of cooperation that continue to exist must not be at the expense of the firmness and unity that we must contribute to through the EU and NATO in response to Russia's actions in, among other things, Ukraine

[1288] This must be done through an insistence on discussing and negotiating each issue separately and without linking it to other issues. Arctic issues are an area where dialogue and cooperation with Russia have largely been successful, and civil cooperation in the Baltic Sea region could be another

[1289] Here too, Denmark will be able to play a constructive role in maintaining the dialogue on selected topics of common interest with Russia, for example through the Baltic Sea Council, and with selected regions, authorities and organizations in Russia

[1290] In addition to dialogue through official, state-to-state channels, it is also in Denmark's interest to counteract the isolation of Russian society by strengthening contact with Russian civil society organizations and supporting people-to-people contacts

[1291] Here, cultural cooperation and exchange in the areas of education and research could also play an active role in order to counter false enemy images and contradictions

[1292] Strategic interests – Russia and Eastern Europe Support for Russia's neighboring countries

[1293] The struggle in Ukraine is not just about territories, but to a large extent also about a choice between two social models in the countries in the EU's eastern neighbourhood: A European model with rules-based and open societies and independent institutions

[1294] Or a post-Soviet model of society with political use of state institutions to ensure the retention of power and economic benefits for a political elite

[1295] It is a showdown between the reforms of the new Ukraine and the corruption and abuse of power of the old Ukraine

[1296] However, there is only a prospect of positive development with Western support and clear demands for reforms in Ukraine

[1297] It is important for Denmark that Europe stands firm on principles of territorial integrity and the freedom of countries to choose their own affiliation

[1298] This means, among other things, that in the dialogue with Russia, arguments must be rejected that Russia has special interests or legitimate spheres of interest in its immediate vicinity that disregard the countries' right to self-determination

[1299] However, a decisive factor for which principles will apply in practice in Denmark's and the EU's immediate area to the east will be whether the eastern neighboring countries succeed in carrying out a successful transformation into politically and economically well-functioning societies

[1300] It is therefore in Denmark's and Europe's interest to support reforms and capacity building in the EU's Eastern partners

[1301] Central in this context is reform support for Ukraine, which has most clearly experienced Russia's encroachment on its territorial integrity, and whose possible successful transition could influence popular demands for similar transformations in the rest of the region, including further east

[1302] A condition for the new

[1303] Ukraine's success is that it has managed to unleash the country's great economic potential and create growth that is comparable to that achieved by Western neighboring countries in the region through their reforms and later EU membership

[1304] Here are: * To maintain European and Western unity and firmness towards Russia, among other things through joint EU sanctions and NATO commitments including active Danish participation in exercises and operations with a view to deterrence * To ensure dialogue with Russia on the basis of established principles of territorial integrity and the right of nation states to self-determination * To identify and safeguard common interests and areas of cooperation with Russia based on Denmark's neighbouring areas

[1305] Strengthen contact and support for civil society, people-to-people contacts and exchanges, for example in cultural, educational and scientific areas. * Taking into account the EU sanctions regime, maintain and develop trade and business relations with Russia

[1306] In the energy area, however, work to limit the EU countries' dependence on Russian energy * To strengthen and decentralize efforts based on the current Neighborhood Program aimed at a smaller number of countries in the EU's eastern neighbourhood * In the long term, work to ease the West's and Denmark's relations with Russia, including through increased dialogue, for example in the Baltic Sea Council and the NATO-Russia Council

[1307] As stated in Chapter 6, a combination of commercial and public/private satellite-based solutions and a general strengthening of the Danish Armed Forces' capabilities in the Arctic region are therefore recommended

[1308] Ukraine's own ambitious reform program and the deep and comprehensive free trade agreement with the EU are essential instruments

[1309] Denmark should continue to contribute actively to Ukraine's reform process through bilateral support programmes and by maintaining EU support for focused and effective reform efforts

[1310] The same applies to other countries in the region, including Belarus in particular

[1311] These activities have so far been supported by the Neighbourhood Programme

[1313] The melting of the ice will create increased activity in areas such as raw material extraction, transport and tourism, and an increasing need for surveillance, sea rescue and environmental protection will result

[1314] The development will also create greater international interest in the region

[1315] There is an increasing need to develop the existing international framework that ensures cooperation in soft areas such as research, innovation and societal development across the Arctic

[1316] The Kingdom has significant interests in peaceful, stable and economically and environmentally sustainable development in the Arctic and also has a special responsibility and special opportunities to influence development in the Arctic for the benefit of the region and, in particular, the people of Greenland and the Faroe Islands

[1317] The Kingdom must therefore maintain and develop its position as a leading Arctic player and exploit the influence that comes with it

[1318] This requires an increased political and economic focus on the Arctic and the Commonwealth

[1319] Development of an international Arctic research hub in Greenland

[1320] There is increasing international interest in research into climate change and Arctic conditions

[1321] With Greenland's unique conditions, the Kingdom has the opportunity to strengthen its contribution to global climate and environmental research, strengthen its Arctic profile internationally, and contribute to local and sustainable growth in Greenland

[1322] The possibilities for cooperation between Danish and Greenlandic authorities on the development of an Arctic research hub in Greenland should therefore be investigated

[1323] Experience from international research hubs in Svalbard and New Zealand, among others, shows that an increased influx of researchers and research funds has an economic effect, including on tourism and other industries, and can thus support the local economy and employment

[1324] In addition, a research hub in Greenland could become an important element in Danish research diplomacy

[1325] Arctic diplomacy In order to fully exploit the Kingdom's status as an Arctic coastal state, the Kingdom must be able to deliver a professional and visible effort in the area of public diplomacy

[1326] Hosting agenda-setting conferences, international meetings, etc. in Denmark, Greenland and the Faroe Islands is one necessary part, and active participation in other major conferences and events should also be prioritized

[1327] As part of this effort, it is recommended that, no later than the tenth anniversary of the Ilulissat Declaration in 2018, the coastal states be brought together to take stock of the implementation of the declaration and, if necessary, discuss the need for a framework for strengthened security policy cooperation

[1328] The overall aim here is to further strengthen the international legal framework for development in the Arctic and the coastal states' obligation to cooperate within this framework

[1329] Due to its size and location, Greenland has great strategic importance for the Kingdom, which is the world's 12th largest and NATO's third largest land area after Canada and the USA

[1330] The Arctic Strategy as a Common Platform Effective safeguarding of the Kingdom's interests requires that there is a common starting point and a consolidated position on what the Kingdom's goals are in the region, across sectors and across the Kingdom

[1331] The “Kingdom's Arctic Strategy for 2011-2020” today constitutes the common platform where the kingdom's consolidated, common goals of peaceful and sustainable development in the Arctic are stated

[1332] The strategy functions as a collaborative instrument for all stakeholders and authorities and is the basis for a coordinated Arctic policy from the three kingdoms, which maximizes its impact internationally

[1333] This approach should therefore be maintained, and implementation strengthened in light of continued climatic, economic and political developments, including in relation to the formulation of foreign and security policy goals

[1334] New financing mechanisms and increased allocation of employees

[1335] Common to many of the opportunities and obligations that result from the Kingdom's position in the Arctic is that safeguarding interests requires political as well as economic investments

[1336] It is proposed to identify possible financing mechanisms, including opportunities within the Growth Fund, for private foundations and the activation of pension funds in a special Arctic fund

[1337] At the international level, the Kingdom should also explore opportunities for investment in the Arctic, for example through the establishment of an Arctic investment bank

[1338] At the same time, additional employees should be allocated to the subject area in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and possibly in the rest of the central administration, so that, together with the increased Arctic efforts of the Danish Armed Forces, the Arctic region is given political priority

[1339] This will be a prerequisite for realizing the recommended efforts and ensuring the necessary coordination, which, due to the special nature of the Kingdom, is of crucial importance for creating productive cooperation on common objectives

[1340] Communication solutions and the defense's task solving

[1341] The area's size and the expected increased activity create an increasing need for communication solutions and an updated situational picture for the defence's task performance. [1351] Many of the opportunities and challenges resulting from Arctic development must be handled through international cooperation

[1352] There is therefore a need to look at the possibilities for strengthening the multilateral framework for Arctic cooperation

[1353] The Arctic Council has developed into the primary international forum for Arctic issues, particularly in the areas of climate, sustainable development and the environment, and plays a central role in the overall protection of the Kingdom's interests

[1354] The Arctic Council and the other institutions in the region should continue to be strengthened and developed so that the Council maintains its status and is able to handle the challenges and opportunities that development brings

[1355] The opening of new sea areas in the Arctic will increase the need for cooperation and joint regulation in the marine area as a result of increased tourism, transport and fishing

[1356] In the area of ​​fisheries, an agreement was reached in the summer of 2015 between the Arctic coastal states to prevent unregulated fishing on the high seas in the Central Arctic Ocean

[1357] It will be in the Kingdom's interest to work towards more countries joining the agreement and to establish a mechanism for the sustainable exploitation of living marine resources in the future

[1358] Need for a security policy forum

[1359] It follows from the so-called Ottawa Declaration that the Arctic Council does not deal with military security, and therefore there is no institutional framework for handling security policy issues in the Arctic

[1360] In line with the increased military presence and activity, there is a growing need for an intergovernmental structure for handling security issues in the Arctic

[1361] The need is emphasized by the fact that Russia has shown itself elsewhere to be prepared to disregard international rules of the game and use military means, regardless of the fact that this is not considered to be part of Russian thinking in the Arctic

[1362] It should therefore be explored whether support can be generated among the relevant Arctic states for establishing a forum for security policy discussions. Such a forum could in itself have a confidence-building effect and, in the event of periods of high tension, could function as a hotbed for political unrest, radicalization, terrorism, migration and sectarian tensions

[1363] However, Denmark also has aggressive economic interests in the region

[1364] However, the instability means that the potential for economic cooperation will not be fully exploited in the short to medium term. space for security policy dialogue between Russia and a number of Western countries

[1365] Finally, a forum could serve as a platform for establishing further confidencebuilding measures in the region, for example, prior notification of military movements or expansion of military infrastructure

[1366] The need for such a framework will be increasing, partly because of the military presence, and partly because the defense and coast guards of the Arctic countries solve a wide range of civil and emergency tasks that do not have a military purpose. Focused and realistic Middle East policy Danish Middle East policy should take stock of developments and adapt and focus the instruments where we have special interests at stake and can influence the situation in partnership with others

[1367] Denmark must set ambitious but at the same time realistic goals for our foreign policy in the Middle East

[1368] In light of developments in recent decades, it is clear that most countries in the region are unlikely to develop into well-functioning democracies similar to countries in Western Europe in the foreseeable future

[1369] The overall objective in the short and medium term for Denmark should therefore be crisis management, including – bilaterally and through the EU, NATO and the UN – working to slow down and de-escalate the many conflicts that negatively affect the region

[1370] It must contribute to combating violent extremism and terrorism and countering refugee and migration flows, as central priorities for Denmark's and the EU's efforts

[1371] Not least because of the geographical proximity, the security and prosperity of Europe and Denmark in a broad sense cannot avoid being affected by the turbulent situation in the region

[1372] In addition, there are classic, offensive foreign policy interests, including in the area of export promotion

[1373] Danish exports to the Middle East and North Africa in 2015 amounted to 19 billion kroner

[1374] This figure is expected to increase in the coming years, including the opening of the Iranian market after the conclusion of the nuclear agreement

[1375] Due to the complexity of the challenges facing the region, there is a need for interaction between several instruments: stabilization efforts and military means, foreign policy efforts, humanitarian assistance and development cooperation

[1376] Which instruments are used in relation to which countries and situations should reflect a strategic prioritization that weighs Danish interests, the needs of the individual countries, our possibilities for influence, and the commitment of the EU, the UN, and other organizations and countries

[1377] The breadth of our engagement in relation to large, leading regional countries such as Saudi Arabia, Iran, Israel and Egypt should be significantly greater than in relation to, for example, smaller Gulf countries

[1378] For the latter, the main focus will be predominantly on economic diplomacy and export promotion

[1379] Without constructive engagement from the regional powers, it will not be possible to find sustainable solutions to the region's many challenges and conflicts, including getting the destabilizing Sunni-Shia conflict onto a political track

[1380] The continental shelf issue The Kingdom and Russia have, under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, claimed the extension of their continental shelves in the Arctic, and there is a large overlap between the two claims

[1381] For procedural reasons, Russia's claims will be processed within a shorter time horizon, while the Kingdom's will only be processed within a longer period of years

[1382] It is therefore proposed, in cooperation with other interested countries, to explore the possibilities of identifying other possible – and faster – models for a solution, including by accelerating the work of the Continental Shelf Commission

[1383] It is in the interest of both the Kingdom and the other Arctic coastal states to ensure that the issue of border demarcation in the Arctic is resolved through negotiations on the basis of the law of the sea, including the recommendations of the Danish Continental Shelf Commission

[1384] There is therefore a task in maintaining an ongoing and constructive dialogue with Russia, Canada and the other nations on border demarcation and maintaining focus on the negotiation track. * To promote peaceful and environmentally and economically sustainable development in the Arctic region * To strengthen the multilateral framework for international Arctic cooperation and contribute to continued dialogue and cooperation between the Arctic states, peoples and organizations * To strengthen the Kingdom’s Arctic profile with a view to maximizing its influence on developments in the Arctic for the benefit of the region, the Kingdom and the local population * To ensure a satisfactory and sustainable resolution of the shelf issue

[1813] Strengthened efforts in countries in fragile situations Denmark should strengthen its efforts in countries in fragile situations. Crisis and conflict situations will continue to be complex and long-lasting, resulting in massive refugee and displacement crises and regional destabilization

[1814] Therefore, stronger interaction must be ensured between humanitarian assistance, long-term development efforts, and peace and stabilization efforts

[1815] At the same time, Denmark's efforts should be concentrated on a limited number of countries

[1870] Prevention of migration Efforts

[1871] to stabilise countries in fragile situations and create favourable economic and political development is closely linked to the prevention of future migration flows

[1872] The current refugee and migration crisis has put EU cooperation and Denmark under pressure both politically and economically and has highlighted the need for Danish development cooperation to address challenges related to migration

[1873] Since the early 2000s, Danish development cooperation has focused on refugees and internally displaced persons in areas of crisis and conflict, but to a lesser extent on the part related to economic migration. The migration and development agenda aims to ensure that everyone has the freedom to create a future for themselves and their families where they belong

[1874] The intention is to prevent unregulated, illegal economic migration towards Europe, facilitate positive aspects of migration and limit secondary refugee flows, for example from stays in nearby areas

[1875] Aid to refugees is most cost-effective by strengthening efforts in or close to the countries of origin

[2233] Framework for defence

[2234] The chapter deals with the future task solving of the Danish Armed Forces based on a description of Denmark's strategic framework conditions

[2235] The tasks of the Danish Armed Forces are laid down in the Defence Act, which states that military defence must contribute to promoting peace and security, and that the Danish Armed Forces constitute an important security policy instrument with three purposes: Firstly, to prevent conflicts and war, secondly, to enforce Denmark's sovereignty and ensure the country's continued existence and integrity, and thirdly, to promote peaceful development in the world with respect for human rights

[2236] The Defence Act also states that the defence is an integrated part of NATO, which, in cooperation with allied forces, must be able to participate in conflict prevention, crisis management and defence of NATO's territory

[2237] The Defence Forces must also be able to identify and reject violations of Danish sovereignty and carry out official duties

[2238] In addition, it must be able to participate in solving confidence-building and stability-promoting tasks and enter into dialogue and cooperation with other countries within and outside NATO

[2239] The Defence Act also states that the defence must have forces that have a size, combat power, endurance, mobility and flexibility that make it possible to solve the tasks mentioned

[2240] The military defense is supported by the Home Guard, and it is stated in the Home Guard Act that the Home Guard participates as part of the military defense in solving the defense's tasks and supporting other authorities

[2241] In addition, a number of other authorities fall under the Minister of Defense's jurisdiction, including the Danish Emergency Management Agency and the Danish Defense Intelligence Agency

[2242] These also support or cooperate with the defense as well as with other authorities

[2243] In Denmark, there is a tradition that the framework of defense policy is regulated via five-year political agreements (defense agreements) as well as any ongoing supplementary agreements

[2244] The current agreement runs until the end of

[2245] Similarly, there is a tradition of regulating preparedness through political settlements, just as the Home Guard is regulated as part of the defense settlements

[2261] Among the world's power centers – the United States, the EU, Russia, China, and India – the United States is the only country capable of deploying significant military forces across the globe

[2532] The improved security situation in the wake of the end of the Cold War has had a major impact on the organization of the Danish defense

[2533] The basis for this was laid down in the 2003 ‘Bruun Report’ on ‘

[2534] The security policy conditions for Danish defense policy

[2535] Here it was concluded that the conventional military threat to Danish territory had disappeared for the foreseeable future

[2536] It was also determined that new threats in the future would probably be more asymmetric and unpredictable, and that a main priority for Danish security policy would increasingly be to deploy capabilities for tasks far away

[2537] Based on the Bruun report, the territorial defense was abolished by the defense agreement concluded in

[2538] With this and the later defense agreements, the line was also laid for the adjustments towards an increasingly flexible and adaptable defense that have since been implemented and are still ongoing

[2539] Although the objective of the Bruun report was that Denmark should be able to send integrated force contributions that could carry out independent operations, developments have since shown that Denmark can only operate in cooperation with other NATO and non-NATO countries in international operations

[2540] This has not meant that Denmark has surrendered its freedom of action and has become vulnerable to the decisions of other nations

[2541] Rather, it has meant that Danish defense has developed its capabilities in a way that allows them to participate flexibly and without limitations in operations with other countries

[2542] This approach focuses on ensuring that military capabilities are as flexible as possible in order to handle the highly volatile security challenges

[2543] This has given the government and the Danish Parliament freedom of action and the opportunity to choose between a number of military tools

[2544] This approach has since guided the organization of the Danish Armed Forces and has contributed to Denmark being able to continue to participate in the entire spectrum of international efforts

[2545] In addition, there are national tasks such as surveillance, sovereignty enforcement, search and rescue services, etc., not least in the Arctic

[2547] The Armed Forces must be able to operate effectively across the defence forces and in collaboration with the Home Guard, the emergency services and other authorities, and there will be a need for increased support for the police
